recipes.name: Southern fried chicken
recipes.description: Bone-in chicken soaked overnight in seasoned buttermilk, dredged in a peppery flour coating and fried in a heavy pot until the crust is craggy, deep golden and crisp and the meat stays juicy.
equipment: Large Dutch oven or deep cast-iron skillet
Wire rack set over a baking tray

ingredients.name: Whole chicken (about 1.6 kg)
ingredients.prep: cut into 10 pieces: 2 drumsticks, 2 thighs, 2 wings, breasts halved crosswise

ingredients.name: Vegetable or peanut oil, for frying

steps.t: Pat the chicken pieces dry. In a large bowl whisk the buttermilk with the hot sauce, salt, pepper and garlic powder. Add the chicken, turn to coat, cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours and ideally overnight. The acid and salt season the meat all the way through and keep it juicy.
Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before frying. Lift the pieces into a colander set over the bowl and let the excess buttermilk drip off; keep 3 tablespoons of it and discard the rest.

Whisk the flour, cornflour, baking powder, paprika, garlic and onion powders, cayenne, pepper and salt in a wide bowl. Drizzle in the 3 tablespoons of reserved buttermilk and rub it through with your fingertips until the flour has lots of small, shaggy clumps; these become the craggy crust.

Dredge each piece in the flour, pressing firmly so it sticks and packing more on top, then shake off the loose flour. Set the pieces on the wire rack and leave for 10–15 minutes, until the coating looks damp and pasty. This resting stops the crust falling off in the oil.
Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat to 175 °C; it should be about 4 cm deep and the pot no more than one-third full. Heat the oven to 100 °C to keep the cooked chicken warm.

Fry the dark meat first: lower 4 or 5 pieces into the oil, skin side down, without crowding. The temperature will drop; adjust the heat to keep it at 160–165 °C. Fry for 6–7 minutes, then turn and fry for 6–7 minutes more, until deep golden brown and a thermometer in the thickest part of a thigh reads at least 74 °C (ideally 80 °C for dark meat).

Lift the chicken onto the rack and keep it warm in the oven. Let the oil come back to 175 °C, then fry the breasts and wings the same way; they need 5–6 minutes per side. The juices near the bone should run clear with no pink.

Rest the chicken on the rack for 5–10 minutes so the crust sets and the juices settle; don't stack it or cover it, or the crust will steam soft. Serve hot or at room temperature with buttermilk biscuits, coleslaw, mashed potatoes or collard greens, and more hot sauce or a drizzle of honey.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours in a covered container and eat within 3 days. Fried chicken is also very good cold.
recipes.reheating: Reheat on a rack in a 200 °C oven for 15–20 minutes, until crisp and steaming hot throughout; the microwave makes the crust soggy.
notes: Leave the oil to cool completely, then strain it and keep it in a jar for the next batch, or take it to a recycling point; never pour it down the sink.
Lard or vegetable shortening is the old-fashioned frying fat; shortening gives the same crisp crust and keeps the dish pork-free.

recipes.name: Buttermilk biscuits
recipes.description: Tall, flaky Southern biscuits made with cold butter and tangy buttermilk, folded a few times for layers and baked hot until golden. Serve with butter and honey or alongside fried chicken.
equipment: Baking tray or 25 cm cast-iron skillet

steps.t: Heat the oven to 230 °C with a shelf in the upper third. Line a baking tray with baking paper, or butter a cast-iron skillet. Hot, fast baking is what makes biscuits rise tall.

Whisk the flour, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, sugar and salt together in the large bowl. Grate the frozen butter straight into the flour on the coarse side of the box grater, tossing every so often so the shreds stay separate, or cut cubes of cold butter in with a pastry cutter until the pieces are the size of peas.

Pour in the cold buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy, sticky dough forms and there's no dry flour at the bottom of the bowl. Don't knead: overworking develops gluten and makes biscuits tough.

Tip the dough onto a floured surface and pat it into a rectangle about 2 cm thick. Fold it in thirds like a letter, turn it 90 degrees and pat it out again. Repeat the folding twice more; these folds stack the butter into thin layers that puff apart in the oven.

Pat the dough out to 2.5 cm thick. Dip the cutter in flour and cut straight down without twisting (twisting seals the edges and stops the rise). Place the biscuits on the tray just touching each other so they help each other climb. Press the scraps together gently and cut again.

Brush the tops with a little buttermilk and bake for 12–15 minutes, until risen, deep golden on top and the sides look dry and flaky. A biscuit broken open should be fluffy, not doughy, in the middle.
Brush the hot biscuits with melted butter and leave them for a few minutes. Serve warm, split and spread with butter, honey or jam, or alongside fried chicken, gravy or eggs.

recipes.storage: Best on the day. Keep airtight at room temperature for up to 2 days, or freeze baked or unbaked biscuits for up to 3 months (bake frozen ones for 2–3 minutes longer).
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 180 °C oven for 5–8 minutes.

recipes.name: Baked macaroni and cheese
recipes.description: Soul-food style baked macaroni in a rich sharp-cheddar sauce made with evaporated milk and set with eggs, so it slices into creamy squares under a golden cheesy top.

ingredients.name: Paprika
ingredients.prep: half in the sauce, half for the top

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.prep: plus more for the pasta water

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C and butter the baking dish. Bring the large pot of well-salted water to the boil and cook the macaroni for 2 minutes less than the packet says, so it is still firm in the centre; it finishes cooking in the oven. Drain without rinsing and tip back into the pot.

Make a roux, the flour-and-butter base that thickens the sauce: melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat, whisk in the flour and cook, whisking, for 1–2 minutes until it smells biscuity but hasn't coloured.

Slowly pour in the warm milk and then the evaporated milk, whisking all the time so no lumps form. Simmer gently for 4–5 minutes, whisking often, until the sauce is smooth and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

Take the pan off the heat and stir in the 300 g of cheese a handful at a time until melted, then the mustard, onion powder, half the paprika, the pepper and salt. Taste: it should be well seasoned and sharp.

Temper the eggs so they don't scramble: whisk a ladleful of the hot sauce into the beaten eggs, then stir the egg mixture back into the sauce. Pour the sauce over the macaroni and fold until every piece is coated.
Spread the macaroni in the dish, scatter over the remaining cheese and dust with the rest of the paprika. Bake for 30–35 minutes, until bubbling at the edges and golden brown on top.
Let it rest for 10–15 minutes before serving so the sauce sets and it cuts into neat, creamy squares. Serve as a side with fried chicken, collard greens, barbecue or a holiday roast.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat portions covered in a 180 °C oven with a splash of milk for 15–20 minutes, until steaming hot.

recipes.name: Chicken and sausage gumbo
recipes.description: Cajun gumbo built on a slow-cooked, chocolate-dark roux and the 'holy trinity' of onion, pepper and celery, simmered with chicken thighs and smoked sausage and ladled over white rice.
equipment: Large heavy Dutch oven (6 litres or more)
Saucepan with lid, for the rice

steps.t: Get everything ready before you start, because the roux can't be left: dice the onions, peppers and celery into a bowl, mince the garlic, slice the sausage and cut up the chicken. Mix the Cajun seasoning spices in a small bowl and toss the chicken with half of them and ½ teaspoon of the salt.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the sausage for 4–5 minutes; lift it out. Brown the chicken in two batches for 5–6 minutes each, until golden on most sides, and set it aside with the sausage. It doesn't need to be cooked through.

Make the roux: add the rest of the oil to the pot, lower the heat to medium and whisk in the flour. Cook it, stirring constantly with the flat wooden spoon and scraping the whole base, for 30–45 minutes. It will go from beige to peanut butter to milk chocolate and finally the colour of dark chocolate, smelling deeply nutty. A roux is just flour toasted in fat; the darker it goes, the more flavour and the less thickening it gives. If you see black specks or smell burning, start again.

As soon as the roux is dark, tip in the onions, peppers and celery all at once; this stops the roux cooking further. Stir for 6–8 minutes, until the vegetables are soft, then add the garlic for 1 minute.
Ladle in the warm stock a little at a time, stirring well after each addition so the roux dissolves without lumps. Add the remaining seasoning and the bay leaves and bring to the boil.

Return the chicken, sausage and any juices. Lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes, stirring now and then and skimming off the oil that rises to the surface, until the chicken is very tender and the gumbo has the body of a thin gravy.

While the gumbo simmers, rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then cook it with 600 ml water and a pinch of salt: bring to the boil, cover, cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes and rest off the heat for 10 minutes.

Remove the bay leaves. Stir in the spring onions, parsley and hot sauce, then taste and add salt; the sausage is salty, so season at the end. Serve in deep bowls over a scoop of rice, with more hot sauce at the table.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours (the rice within 1 hour) for up to 4 days, or freeze the gumbo without rice for up to 3 months. It tastes even better the next day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Andouille pork sausage is traditional in Louisiana; smoked beef sausage keeps the gumbo pork-free with the same smoky depth.
Filé powder (ground sassafras leaves), if you have it, is sprinkled into each bowl at the table; it thickens slightly and must not be boiled.

recipes.name: Shrimp and grits
recipes.description: Slow-cooked creamy cheese grits topped with spicy seared shrimp in a garlicky pan gravy with lemon and spring onions, the Lowcountry classic from coastal South Carolina and Georgia.

steps.t: Bring the water, milk and salt to a simmer in the heavy saucepan over medium heat. Pour in the grits in a slow stream, whisking constantly, and keep whisking for about 5 minutes as they thicken so no lumps form.

Turn the heat to low, cover and cook for 40–45 minutes, stirring well every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom, until the grits are thick, creamy and tender with no raw grittiness. Add a splash of hot water if they get too stiff. Stir in the butter and cheese at the end, cover and keep warm.

While the grits cook, pat the prawns dry and toss them with the paprika, cayenne, garlic powder, black pepper and a pinch of salt. If using bacon, fry it in the frying pan over medium heat for 6–8 minutes until crisp, lift it out and keep 1 tablespoon of the fat in the pan in place of the oil.

Heat the oil (or bacon fat) and butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat until the butter foams. Add the prawns in one layer and sear for about 1 minute per side, until just pink; lift them onto a plate. They will finish cooking in the gravy.

Lower the heat to medium. Add the spring onion whites and garlic and stir for 1 minute until soft and fragrant, then sprinkle in the flour and stir for 1 minute more. Whisk in the stock, scraping up the browned bits, and simmer for 2 minutes until it turns into a glossy, lightly thickened gravy. Add the lemon juice and hot sauce.
Return the prawns and their juices and cook for 1 minute, turning them in the gravy, until opaque and curled into a loose C shape; a tight O shape means they're overcooked. Taste and add salt.
Spoon the grits into warm shallow bowls, top with the prawns and gravy and scatter over the spring onion greens, parsley and crumbled bacon, if using. Serve straight away.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Loosen the grits with a splash of milk over low heat, stirring; warm the prawns gently just until hot so they don't toughen.
notes: Quick-cooking grits are ready in about 5–10 minutes; stone-ground grits take longer but have a much better corn flavour and texture.

recipes.name: New England clam chowder
recipes.description: A creamy chowder of fresh clams, potatoes, onion and celery in a thyme-scented broth made from the clams' own juices, finished with milk and cream.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid
Fine sieve lined with muslin or kitchen paper

ingredients.name: Fresh clams in the shell (littlenecks or cherrystones)
Fish stock or bottled clam juice
Waxy or all-purpose potatoes (such as Yukon Gold)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1.5 cm cubes

ingredients.name: Streaky bacon, diced
ingredients.prep: fried at the start for a smoky chowder

steps.t: Scrub the clams under cold running water and discard any with cracked shells or that stay open when tapped. Put them in the large pot with the water, cover and cook over high heat for 6–10 minutes, shaking the pot now and then, until the shells open.

Lift the clams into a bowl with a slotted spoon and discard any that stayed closed. Pour the cooking liquid through the lined sieve into a jug to catch any sand; you should have about 600 ml of briny broth. When the clams are cool enough to handle, pull out the meat and chop it into bite-sized pieces. Rinse out the pot.

If using bacon, fry it in the pot over medium heat for 6–8 minutes until crisp and lift it out, leaving the fat. Melt the butter in the pot over medium-low heat and cook the onion and celery for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not browned.

Sprinkle in the flour and stir for 2 minutes to cook out its raw taste. Gradually whisk in the clam broth and the fish stock so it stays smooth, then add the potatoes, thyme and bay leaf. Bring to the boil, then simmer gently for 12–15 minutes, until the potatoes are just tender to a knife.

Pour in the milk and cream and heat gently, stirring, until steaming with a few small bubbles at the edge; don't let it boil hard or the dairy can split. Add the chopped clams and pepper and warm through for 2 minutes. Clams turn rubbery if they cook any longer.

Remove the thyme stalks and bay leaf and taste before adding salt, as the clam broth is already salty. Take the pot off the heat and leave the chowder to stand for 10 minutes; it thickens slightly as it rests, and it's even better made a few hours ahead.
Ladle into warm bowls and finish with parsley or chives and the crumbled bacon, if using. Serve with oyster crackers or crusty bread.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 2 days. Don't freeze: the potatoes turn grainy and the cream may split.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently over low heat, stirring, until steaming; don't let it boil.

recipes.name: Texas chili con carne
recipes.description: Texas-style 'bowl of red': chunks of beef chuck slowly braised in a sauce of toasted dried chillies, cumin and garlic, thickened with masa. No beans, no mince.

ingredients.name: Beef chuck
ingredients.prep: trimmed and cut into 2 cm cubes

ingredients.name: Dried chiles de árbol
ingredients.prep: for heat; use more or fewer

steps.t: Toast the chillies: heat the dry frying pan over medium heat and press the stemmed, seeded anchos, guajillos and árbols flat in the pan for 20–30 seconds per side, until they smell fragrant and turn pliable and slightly darker. Don't let them blacken or the chili will taste bitter.

Put the toasted chillies in a bowl, pour over 500 ml of the hot stock and leave to soak for 20 minutes, until soft. Blend the chillies and their liquid with the garlic, cumin and oregano until completely smooth, then push the purée through the sieve to remove the tough skins.

Pat the beef dry and season it with 1 teaspoon of the salt. Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the beef in three batches, 4–5 minutes per batch, turning once a deep brown crust forms. Don't crowd the pot or the meat will steam. Set the browned beef aside.

Lower the heat to medium, add the onion and cook for 5 minutes, scraping up the browned bits from the base. Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then pour in the chilli purée and fry it, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it darkens and smells toasty.

Return the beef and its juices with the remaining 500 ml stock and the bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, partly cover and cook on the lowest heat for 2½–3 hours, stirring every 20–30 minutes and adding a splash of water if it gets too thick, until the beef is tender enough to cut with a spoon.

Stir in the masa paste and simmer uncovered for 10 minutes; it thickens the chili and adds a toasted-corn flavour. Season with the vinegar, sugar and remaining salt, then taste and adjust; it should be rich, earthy and warmly spicy.

Remove the bay leaves and rest the chili for 15 minutes off the heat (or make it a day ahead; it gets better). Serve in bowls with chopped onion, and cheese and soured cream if you like, with cornbread, saltine crackers or rice. Beans, if you want them, go on the side.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months; the flavour improves overnight.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Apple pie
recipes.description: A double-crust pie with flaky all-butter pastry and a deep filling of cinnamon-spiced apples that bakes until thick and bubbling. Serve warm with vanilla ice cream.

ingredients.name: Ice-cold water
ingredients.prep: you may not need it all

ingredients.name: Apples, a mix of tart and sweet (such as Granny Smith and Honeycrisp)
ingredients.prep: about 7, peeled, cored and sliced 5 mm thick

ingredients.name: Egg
ingredients.prep: beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for glazing

steps.t: Make the pastry: whisk the flour, sugar and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold butter and cut it in with the pastry cutter (or rub it in quickly with your fingertips) until most of it is the size of peas with some almond-sized pieces left. Those flat bits of butter are what make the crust flaky.

Mix the iced water with the vinegar and sprinkle it over a few tablespoons at a time, tossing with a fork, until the dough holds together when you squeeze a handful. Divide in two, press each half into a flat disc, wrap and chill for at least 1 hour (or up to 2 days) so the butter firms up and the gluten relaxes.
Toss the sliced apples with both sugars, the flour, cinnamon, nutmeg, lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Leave for 20 minutes while you roll the pastry; the apples will start to release juice.

On a floured surface roll one disc into a 30 cm circle about 3 mm thick, turning it often so it doesn't stick. Ease it into the pie dish without stretching (stretched pastry shrinks), leaving the edge overhanging. Pile in the apples and their juices, mounding them in the middle, and dot with the butter.

Roll the second disc to a 28 cm circle and lay it over the filling. Trim both layers to a 2 cm overhang, fold the edge under itself and crimp with your fingers or a fork. Cut 4 or 5 slits in the top for steam, brush with the egg glaze and sprinkle with sugar. Chill for 15 minutes while the oven heats to 220 °C with a baking tray on the lowest shelf.

Bake the pie on the hot tray for 20 minutes, until the pastry is set and starting to colour; the hot tray helps the base crisp. Lower the oven to 190 °C and bake for 40–50 minutes more, until the crust is deep golden and the juices bubble thickly through the slits. Cover the edge with foil if it browns too fast.

Cool the pie on the wire rack for at least 3 hours so the filling thickens; cut it hot and the juices will run everywhere. Serve just warm or at room temperature, with vanilla ice cream, whipped cream or a slice of sharp cheddar.

recipes.storage: Keep loosely covered at room temperature for up to 2 days, then refrigerate for up to 2 days more.
recipes.reheating: Warm slices in a 160 °C oven for 10–15 minutes.

recipes.name: Chocolate chip cookies
recipes.description: Classic American chocolate chip cookies with crisp golden edges, soft chewy centres and plenty of semisweet chocolate, made with creamed butter and brown sugar.
equipment: Electric mixer or large bowl and wooden spoon

steps.t: Heat the oven to 190 °C and line the baking trays with baking paper. Whisk the flour, bicarbonate of soda and salt together in a bowl.
Beat the soft butter with both sugars for 2–3 minutes, until paler, fluffy and creamy. Creaming beats in air, which gives the cookies lift and their chewy-crisp texture.

Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla, scraping down the bowl so everything is evenly mixed. Add the flour mixture and mix on low speed or by hand just until no dry streaks remain; overmixing makes tough cookies. Fold in the chocolate and nuts, if using.

Scoop rounded 2-tablespoon balls of dough onto the trays, about 5 cm apart, as they spread. For thicker, more toffee-flavoured cookies, chill the scooped dough for 30 minutes or up to 2 days before baking.

Bake one tray at a time in the middle of the oven for 9–11 minutes, until the edges are golden brown but the centres still look pale and slightly underdone. They firm up as they cool; baking until the middle looks done gives hard cookies.
Leave the cookies on the tray for 5 minutes, then move them to the wire rack. Serve warm, when the chocolate is still soft, or cooled with a glass of cold milk.

recipes.storage: Keep airtight at room temperature for up to 5 days. Freeze balls of dough for up to 3 months and bake from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes.

recipes.name: Ahi poke bowl
recipes.description: Cubes of raw sashimi-grade tuna tossed in shoyu, sesame oil, sweet onion and spring onion, served Hawaiian-style over warm rice with cucumber, avocado and edamame.

steps.t: Rinse the rice in a sieve under cold water until it runs almost clear. Put it in the saucepan with 360 ml water, bring to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Leave it covered off the heat for 10 minutes, then fluff it and let it cool to just warm.

Keep the tuna in the fridge until the last moment. With a very sharp knife, cut it into 2 cm cubes, slicing cleanly rather than sawing so the edges stay neat. Put the cubes in the bowl set over a larger bowl of ice.
Whisk the soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger and chilli flakes together. Rinse the sliced onion briefly in cold water and drain well to soften its bite.

Add the onion, spring onions and sauce to the tuna and fold gently with a spoon until every cube is glossy. Scatter over the sesame seeds. Refrigerate for 10–15 minutes so the flavours soak in, but no longer: soy starts to cure the fish and change its texture.

Divide the warm rice between four bowls. Spoon the poke on top and arrange the cucumber, avocado and edamame around it. Finish with strips of nori and serve straight away, while the fish is cold and the rice is warm.
If you're making poke for a gathering, serve it in a chilled bowl on its own with rice on the side, and keep it on ice; raw fish shouldn't sit at room temperature for more than an hour.

recipes.storage: Eat poke within a few hours of making it, keeping it chilled; don't keep leftovers of the raw fish.
notes: In Hawaii, poke is often seasoned with limu (seaweed) and inamona (roasted kukui nut); toasted sesame seeds are the easiest substitute.

recipes.name: Poutine
recipes.description: Québec's favourite late-night dish: double-fried chips topped with squeaky fresh cheese curds and a hot, peppery brown gravy that melts the curds just at the edges.

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (russet or Maris Piper)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1 cm batons

ingredients.name: Vegetable or peanut oil, for frying

steps.t: Rinse the potato batons, then soak them in a bowl of cold water for 30 minutes to wash off surface starch; this makes them crisp. Drain and dry them very thoroughly on a clean tea towel, since wet chips make the oil spit. Take the cheese curds out of the fridge now; cold curds won't soften.

Make the gravy: melt the butter in the small saucepan over medium heat, whisk in the flour and cook, whisking, for 3–4 minutes until this roux turns the colour of peanut butter. Add the garlic for 30 seconds.

Gradually whisk in both stocks, then the ketchup, Worcestershire sauce and pepper. Simmer for 8–10 minutes, whisking now and then, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon. Taste for salt and keep it hot on the lowest heat: it must be very hot to soften the curds.

Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 160 °C (no more than one-third full). Fry the chips in three batches for 5–6 minutes each, until soft and pale but not coloured. Lift onto the rack and let them cool for at least 10 minutes. This first fry cooks the inside.
Raise the oil to 190 °C and fry the chips again in batches for 2–3 minutes, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on the rack and sprinkle with salt.

Pile the hot chips into four bowls, scatter over the cheese curds, tearing any big ones, and pour the hot gravy over the top. The curds should soften and turn stretchy at the edges while keeping their squeak in the middle. Serve straight away with forks.

recipes.storage: Poutine doesn't keep: assemble it just before eating. Leftover gravy keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Bring the gravy back to the boil before pouring it over freshly fried chips.
notes: Squeaky cheese curds are fresh, unaged cheddar curds; if you can't find them, torn pieces of a mild, fresh mozzarella are the closest substitute.

recipes.name: Soupe aux pois (Québec split pea soup)
recipes.description: A thick, golden soup of yellow split peas slowly simmered with onion, carrot, celery, bay and savoury herbs until the peas collapse. A budget classic from Québec's farmhouse kitchens.

ingredients.name: Smoked ham hock
ingredients.prep: the traditional version: simmer it with the peas and shred the meat back in

steps.t: Rinse the split peas in a sieve and pick out any small stones. Soaking isn't necessary, but peas soaked overnight in cold water will cook about 30 minutes faster.

Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrots and celery and cook gently, stirring now and then, for 8–10 minutes, until soft and sweet but not browned. Add the garlic for 1 minute.
Add the peas, stock, water, bay leaves, savory or thyme, smoked paprika and pepper (and the ham hock, if using). Bring to the boil and skim off the foam that rises to the top with a large spoon.

Lower the heat, partly cover and simmer very gently for 1½–2 hours, stirring every 15 minutes and scraping the base, as split peas like to catch. The soup is ready when the peas have completely broken down and it is thick and creamy.
Remove the bay leaves. Leave the soup rustic, or mash or blend about half of it for a smoother texture. It thickens a lot as it stands, so loosen it with hot water until it pours slowly from a ladle.
Season with salt only now, tasting as you go, because stock varies in saltiness. Serve hot, sprinkled with parsley, with crusty bread or buttered rye.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. It sets firm when cold; loosen with water when reheating.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Québec cooks traditionally simmer the soup with a smoked ham hock; smoked paprika gives a gentle smokiness without meat.

recipes.name: Maple-glazed salmon
recipes.description: Salmon fillets brushed with a sticky glaze of pure maple syrup, soy sauce, mustard and garlic, roasted until just flaky and glossy. A quick weeknight favourite across Canada.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C and line the baking tray with baking paper, brushed with the oil so the skin doesn't stick.

Whisk the maple syrup, soy sauce, mustard, garlic and lemon juice in the small saucepan. Pour half into a small bowl for brushing. Simmer the rest over medium heat for 3–4 minutes, until reduced by about a third and syrupy; this becomes the sauce for serving.
Pat the salmon dry, season lightly with salt and pepper and lay it skin side down on the tray. Brush generously with the unreduced glaze.
Roast for 10–12 minutes, brushing with the glaze again halfway, until the salmon is opaque, flakes easily when pressed and reaches 63 °C in the thickest part. Thinner fillets will be done sooner.
For a deeper caramelised top, switch the grill on high for the last 1–2 minutes and watch closely, as the maple sugars burn quickly.
Rest the salmon for 2 minutes, spoon over the reduced glaze and scatter with chives. Serve with rice or roasted potatoes and green beans, asparagus or a crisp salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Eat leftovers cold, flaked into salads or rice bowls, or warm gently in a 150 °C oven for about 10 minutes; high heat dries it out.

recipes.name: Chilaquiles rojos
recipes.description: Crisp fried tortilla wedges tossed in a smoky guajillo and tomato salsa, topped with crema, crumbled fresh cheese, onion, coriander and a fried egg. Mexico's favourite breakfast.

ingredients.name: Corn tortillas, preferably a day old

steps.t: If your tortillas are fresh, spread the wedges on a tray and dry them in a 150 °C oven for 10 minutes, or leave them out for a few hours; dry tortillas absorb less oil and stay crisper.

Make the salsa: put the tomatoes, guajillos, árbol chilli, onion and garlic in the saucepan, cover with water and simmer for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes are soft and the chillies pliable. Lift them out with the slotted spoon and blend with the stock and salt until smooth.

Heat the oil in the deep frying pan to about 180 °C (a tortilla wedge should sizzle immediately). Fry the wedges in batches for 1–2 minutes, turning, until golden and crisp; the bubbling slows when they're ready. Drain on kitchen paper and sprinkle with a little salt.

Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of the oil (keep a little for the eggs). Return the pan to medium-high heat and carefully pour in the salsa; it will spatter. Fry it, stirring, for 4–5 minutes, until it darkens and thickens slightly. Taste for salt.
Meanwhile fry the eggs in another pan with a little of the reserved oil over medium heat for 3–4 minutes, until the whites are set and the edges lacy.

Add the tortilla chips to the salsa and toss for 30 seconds to 1 minute, just until coated, if you like them with some crunch, or a few minutes longer for soft chilaquiles. Divide between plates and top each with a fried egg, crema, queso fresco, onion rings, coriander and avocado, if using. Serve immediately, with refried beans on the side.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; the chips soften as they sit. Leftover salsa keeps refrigerated for up to 5 days.

recipes.name: Huevos rancheros
recipes.description: Ranch-style eggs: fried eggs on lightly fried corn tortillas spread with refried beans, spooned with a charred tomato and chilli salsa and finished with fresh cheese and coriander.

steps.t: Char the salsa vegetables: heat the dry frying pan or comal over high heat and roast the tomatoes, chilli, onion slices and garlic, turning occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until blistered and blackened in patches and softened. Peel the garlic and pull the stem off the chilli.

Blend the charred vegetables with the salt to a slightly chunky salsa. Heat 1 teaspoon of the oil in the small saucepan, pour in the salsa (it will spatter) and simmer for 5 minutes until slightly thickened. Keep warm.
Warm the beans in a pan with a splash of their liquid and mash them roughly with a fork or masher into a thick, spreadable refried bean paste. Season with a pinch of salt and keep warm.

Wipe out the frying pan, add 1 tablespoon of oil and heat over medium-high. Fry the tortillas one at a time for 20–30 seconds per side, until softened and lightly blistered but still pliable. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm under a tea towel.
Add the remaining oil to the pan and fry the eggs over medium heat, a few at a time, for 3–4 minutes, spooning hot oil over the whites until they are set and the yolks are still runny.

Put two tortillas on each plate, spread with beans and top with two eggs. Spoon the warm salsa around and over the whites (leaving the yolks showing), then scatter with queso fresco and coriander and add avocado if you like. Serve at once.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly made. Leftover salsa keeps refrigerated for up to 5 days and refried beans for 3 days.

recipes.name: Enchiladas verdes
recipes.description: Soft corn tortillas rolled around shredded chicken and smothered in a tangy tomatillo and serrano salsa, finished with crema, crumbled cheese and raw onion.

steps.t: Put the chicken in the saucepan with the quarter onion, garlic, salt and about 1 litre of water. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 15–18 minutes, until the thickest part reaches 74 °C. Let the chicken cool in the broth for 10 minutes, then lift it out and shred it with two forks. Keep 250 ml of the broth.

Make the salsa: put the tomatillos and serranos in a pan, cover with water and simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the tomatillos turn from bright to olive green and are soft but not bursting. Drain and blend with the half onion, garlic, coriander, salt and the reserved chicken broth until smooth.

Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in the wide frying pan over medium-high heat, pour in the salsa carefully (it spatters) and simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until it thickens slightly and turns a deeper green. Taste for salt and keep it warm over low heat.

Heat the 3 tablespoons of oil in the small frying pan over medium heat. Pass each tortilla through the oil for 5–10 seconds per side so it turns soft and pliable without crisping, and drain on kitchen paper. This stops them cracking and turning soggy in the sauce.
One at a time, dip each tortilla into the warm salsa, lay it on a plate, put a line of shredded chicken across it and roll it up. Arrange three enchiladas, seam side down, on each warmed plate.

Spoon plenty of hot salsa over the enchiladas, drizzle with crema and scatter with queso fresco, sliced onion and coriander leaves. Serve straight away, with Mexican rice and refried beans if you like.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered in a 180 °C oven for 15–20 minutes until steaming hot; the tortillas soften as they sit.

recipes.name: Chiles rellenos (cheese-stuffed poblanos)
recipes.description: Roasted, peeled poblano chillies stuffed with melting cheese, coated in a cloud-like egg batter, fried until golden and served in a light, oregano-scented tomato broth.

ingredients.name: Queso Oaxaca or Chihuahua (or low-moisture mozzarella)
Plain flour
ingredients.prep: for dredging, plus 1 tbsp for the batter

steps.t: Roast the poblanos directly over a gas flame or close under a very hot grill, turning with tongs, for 6–10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and blackened all over but the flesh is still firm. Put them in a bowl, cover with a plate and leave to steam for 15 minutes; this loosens the skins.

Rub off the charred skin with your fingers (don't rinse them, or you'll wash away the smoky flavour). Cut a slit down one side of each chilli, leaving the stem on, and carefully pull out the seed pod and veins. Rinse your hands afterwards: the veins can be hot.

Make the caldillo: blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic until smooth. Heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat, pour in the purée and fry for 5 minutes until it darkens slightly. Add the stock, oregano, bay leaf and salt and simmer for 10 minutes into a light, brothy sauce. Keep it warm.

Stuff each chilli with cheese strips, overlap the edges of the slit and pin it closed with a toothpick. Pat the chillies dry with kitchen paper (the batter won't stick to a wet surface), then roll them in the flour and tap off the excess.

Heat the oil in the deep frying pan to 180 °C, about 2 cm deep. Meanwhile make the capeado batter: whisk the egg whites with the salt to stiff peaks, then whisk in the yolks one at a time and finally fold in 1 tablespoon of flour. It should be thick and airy; use it straight away before it deflates.

Hold a chilli by the stem, dip it into the batter to coat it completely and lay it gently in the oil. Fry 2 or 3 at a time for 2–3 minutes per side, spooning hot oil over the top, until puffed and golden all over. Drain on kitchen paper and remove the toothpicks.
Ladle the hot caldillo into shallow bowls and set a chile relleno in each one; the cheese inside should be molten. Serve straight away with Mexican rice and warm corn tortillas.

recipes.storage: Best freshly fried. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm in the caldillo, covered, over low heat or in a 180 °C oven until the cheese has melted again and everything is steaming.
notes: For picadillo-stuffed chiles rellenos, fill them with beef mince cooked with onion, tomato, raisins and almonds instead of cheese.

recipes.name: Mole poblano with chicken
recipes.description: Puebla's celebration mole: three kinds of dried chilli, toasted nuts, seeds, spices, plantain and a little chocolate ground into a dark, glossy sauce and slowly simmered with poached chicken.

ingredients.name: Chicken pieces, bone-in, skinless (thighs and drumsticks)
Dark chocolate (or 60 g Mexican table chocolate, and no sugar)

steps.t: Poach the chicken: put it in the large pot with the quarter onion, 2 garlic cloves, salt and 2.5 litres of water. Bring to a simmer, skim, and cook gently for 35–40 minutes, until the thickest piece reaches 74 °C. Lift the chicken out and keep it covered; strain the broth. You'll need about 1.5 litres for the mole.

Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium-low heat. Fry the dried chillies a few at a time for 10–15 seconds per side, pressing them flat, until they blister and smell fruity. Don't let them blacken or the mole turns bitter. Put them in a bowl with 750 ml of hot broth and soak for 20 minutes.

In the same pan, with a little more oil, fry each ingredient separately and move it to a big bowl as it's done: the almonds and peanuts for 2–3 minutes until golden; the raisins for 30 seconds until plump; the plantain for 3–4 minutes until browned; then the tortilla and bread for 1–2 minutes until crisp.

Wipe the pan and toast the sesame seeds dry for 2 minutes until golden (set 1 tablespoon aside for garnish), then the whole spices for 1 minute until fragrant. Finally char the tomatoes, tomatillos, onion slices and garlic in the dry pan for 8–10 minutes until blackened in spots; peel the garlic.

Blend the soaked chillies with their broth until completely smooth. Separately blend the nuts, seeds, fruit, bread, tortilla, spices and charred vegetables with 500 ml of broth, in batches, for 2–3 minutes each until very smooth. For a silky mole, push both purées through the sieve.

Heat the remaining oil in the casserole over medium-high heat. Pour in the chilli purée (it will spit) and fry, stirring constantly, for 5 minutes until it darkens and thickens. Add the nut purée and cook for 10 minutes more, stirring and scraping the base, as it catches easily.

Stir in the chocolate, sugar and salt and enough broth (about 250–500 ml) to make a sauce that thickly coats a spoon. Simmer on low heat for 30–45 minutes, stirring often, until dark and glossy with small pools of red oil on the surface. Taste: it should be rich, slightly sweet, gently spicy and well salted.

Meanwhile cook the rice: rinse it, then simmer with 650 ml water and a pinch of salt, covered, on low heat for 15 minutes and rest for 10. Add the chicken to the mole and simmer for 10 minutes until heated through. Serve with rice, warm tortillas and the reserved sesame seeds scattered on top.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 4 days. Mole sauce on its own keeps for a week in the fridge and freezes for up to 6 months; it improves after a day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, stirring, with a splash of broth or water, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Making mole over two days is traditional: poach the chicken and make the sauce on the first day, then reheat and combine on the second.

recipes.name: Elote (Mexican street corn)
recipes.description: Grilled corn on the cob slathered with mayonnaise and crema, rolled in crumbly salty cheese and dusted with chilli and lime, as sold from street carts all over Mexico.
equipment: Barbecue, griddle pan or gas flame

ingredients.name: Cotija cheese (or queso fresco or feta)
Chile piquín or other ground chilli

steps.t: Heat the barbecue, griddle pan or a gas burner to high. Push a skewer into the base of each cob if you want handles.

Grill the corn for 10–12 minutes, turning a quarter turn every 2–3 minutes, until the kernels are tender and charred in patches all round. On a gas flame it takes 5–6 minutes; keep turning so it chars rather than burns.
While the corn cooks, mix the mayonnaise, crema and garlic in a small bowl. Spread the crumbled cheese on a plate.
Brush each hot cob all over with the mayonnaise mixture, then roll it in the cheese, pressing so it sticks. Sprinkle with chilli, a pinch of salt and the coriander.
Serve straight away with lime wedges to squeeze over. For esquites, cut the grilled kernels off the cob and toss them with the same toppings in a cup.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot off the grill. Refrigerate leftover grilled corn for up to 3 days and cut the kernels off for salads or esquites.

recipes.name: Horchata (rice and cinnamon drink)
recipes.description: A cool, creamy-tasting agua fresca made by soaking rice with cinnamon, blending it smooth and straining, then sweetening with sugar and vanilla. Serve over plenty of ice.

ingredients.name: Whole milk, for a creamier horchata
Blanched almonds, soaked with the rice

steps.t: Put the rinsed rice and broken cinnamon sticks in the large bowl and pour over the hot water. Cover and leave to soak at room temperature for at least 4 hours, or overnight in the fridge. The rice softens enough to blend into a milky liquid.
Tip the rice, cinnamon and all the soaking water into the blender and blend on high for 2–3 minutes, until the rice is completely pulverised and the liquid looks chalky white with no visible grains.

Line the sieve with a double layer of muslin and set it over the jug. Pour the mixture through in batches, stirring, then gather up the cloth and squeeze firmly to extract all the liquid. Discard the gritty pulp.
Stir in the cold water, sugar and vanilla (and milk, if using) until the sugar dissolves. Taste: it should be sweet, creamy and fragrant with cinnamon. Chill for at least 1 hour.
The rice starch settles as it stands, so stir well before pouring. Serve in tall glasses over plenty of ice with a light dusting of ground cinnamon, alongside tacos or spicy food.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a covered jug for up to 3 days; stir before pouring as the starch settles.

recipes.name: Birria de res (Jalisco braised beef)
recipes.description: Beef chuck and short ribs braised for hours in a rich adobo of guajillo and ancho chillies, vinegar and warm spices until falling apart, served in its own red consommé with onion, coriander, lime and tortillas.
equipment: Large ovenproof Dutch oven with lid
Heavy dry frying pan or comal

steps.t: Season the beef and short ribs with 1½ teaspoons of the salt. Heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the meat in batches for 4–5 minutes per side until well coloured. Set aside. Heat the oven to 160 °C.

Toast the guajillo, ancho and árbol chillies on the dry pan over medium heat for 15–20 seconds per side, until fragrant and pliable; don't let them scorch. Simmer them in a small pan of water with the tomatoes for 10 minutes until soft, then drain.

Toast the cumin, cloves, cinnamon and peppercorns in the dry pan for 1 minute until fragrant. Blend the chillies, tomatoes, onion, garlic, toasted spices, oregano, thyme, vinegar and 500 ml of the stock until completely smooth, then press through the sieve to remove skins and seeds.

Return the meat to the pot, pour over the adobo and the remaining stock, add the bay leaves and the rest of the salt and stir. For deeper flavour you can cool it and marinate overnight in the fridge at this point. Bring to a simmer on the hob.

Cover tightly and braise in the oven for 3–3½ hours, until the beef falls apart when pressed with a spoon and the short-rib bones slide out. Check halfway and add a little water if the liquid has dropped below the meat.

Lift out the meat, discard the bones and shred it into large pieces. Skim the red fat from the surface of the consommé into a small bowl (keep it for frying tacos). Taste the consommé, add salt if needed, and simmer for 10 minutes.

Serve the beef in bowls with plenty of hot consommé, chopped onion, coriander, lime and warm tortillas. For tacos, dip tortillas in the reserved red fat, crisp them on a hot pan, fill with beef (and cheese, for quesabirria), fold and fry 2 minutes per side, then dunk in a cup of consommé.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the meat in its consommé within 2 hours for up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In Jalisco birria is traditionally made with goat; beef birria (birria de res) is the version popular in Tijuana and across the US.

recipes.name: Pico de gallo
recipes.description: A fresh, chunky salsa of ripe tomato, white onion, serrano chilli and coriander sharpened with lime juice, served with tacos, eggs, grilled meat and tortilla chips.

steps.t: Cut the tomatoes in half and scoop out the watery seeds with a teaspoon if they are very juicy, then dice the flesh into 5 mm pieces. Firm, ripe plum tomatoes give the best texture.

Put the chopped onion in a sieve and rinse it under cold water for a few seconds, then shake dry; this softens its raw bite. Chop the chillies finely, removing the seeds and veins if you want a milder salsa.

Combine the tomatoes, onion, chilli and coriander in the bowl, add the lime juice and salt and toss gently. Taste: it should be bright, fresh and pleasantly hot. Add more lime, salt or chilli as needed.
Leave it for 10–15 minutes so the flavours mingle, then drain off any excess liquid that collects at the bottom. Serve with tacos, quesadillas, eggs, grilled meat or fish, or tortilla chips.

recipes.storage: Best within a few hours. Refrigerate for up to 1 day; the tomatoes soften and release liquid.

recipes.name: Salsa verde cocida (cooked tomatillo salsa)
recipes.description: A tangy green table salsa of simmered tomatillos and serrano chillies blended with raw onion, garlic and coriander, for tacos, eggs, enchiladas and grilled meat.

steps.t: Peel the papery husks off the tomatillos and rinse them well under warm water to remove the sticky coating.

Put the tomatillos and chillies in the saucepan, cover with water and bring to a simmer. Cook for 8–10 minutes, turning them once, until the tomatillos change from bright green to olive green and soften but haven't burst. Burst tomatillos make a watery salsa.

Lift the tomatillos and chillies into the blender with the slotted spoon, keeping the cooking water. Add the onion, garlic, coriander and salt and blend to a slightly chunky or smooth sauce, adding a splash of the cooking water if it's too thick. Vent the blender lid when blending hot food.

Taste and adjust the salt; tomatillos vary in sourness. Let the salsa cool; it thickens slightly as the tomatillos' natural pectin sets. Serve with tacos, eggs, quesadillas, grilled meat or tortilla chips.
For a smoky salsa verde asada, char the tomatillos and chillies in a dry heavy pan or under a hot grill for 8–10 minutes, until blackened in spots and soft, instead of simmering them.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a jar for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.

recipes.name: Baja fish tacos
recipes.description: Strips of white fish in a light, crisp batter, fried and tucked into warm corn tortillas with shredded cabbage, a tangy lime crema and fresh pico de gallo, as sold at the stands of Ensenada.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep frying pan

ingredients.name: Firm white fish fillets (cod, pollock, halibut or mahi-mahi)
Cold lager, in place of the sparkling water

steps.t: Prepare everything that goes on the tacos first, because fried fish waits for no one: shred the cabbage, whisk the mayonnaise, crema and lime juice with a splash of water into a pourable sauce, and mix the tomatoes, onion, chilli, coriander and a pinch of salt into a quick pico de gallo.
Pat the fish strips dry and season them lightly with salt. Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 185 °C; it should be at least 4 cm deep and the pot no more than one-third full.

Whisk the 125 g flour with the baking powder, garlic powder, oregano and salt. Just before frying, whisk in the mustard and the ice-cold sparkling water (or beer) until it is like a thin pancake batter. A few lumps are fine; overmixing makes the coating heavy.

Dust a few fish strips in the dusting flour, dip them in the batter and let the excess drip off, then lower them into the oil, laying them away from you. Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until puffed, crisp and golden and the fish is opaque inside. Drain on the wire rack and fry the rest, letting the oil come back to 180–185 °C between batches.
While the fish fries, warm the tortillas on the hot comal for about 30 seconds per side until soft and spotted, and stack them in a tea towel. Use two tortillas per taco if they are thin.
To serve, put a piece of fish in each tortilla, top with cabbage, a drizzle of lime crema and a spoonful of pico de gallo, and squeeze over lime. Eat straight away while the batter is crisp.

recipes.storage: Best eaten as soon as the fish is fried. Refrigerate leftover fish for up to 1 day and re-crisp it in a hot oven.

recipes.name: Pupusas de frijol con queso (bean and cheese pupusas)
recipes.description: El Salvador's national dish: thick corn-masa rounds stuffed with refried beans and melting cheese, griddled until spotted brown and served with tangy cabbage curtido and a thin tomato salsa.
equipment: Comal, griddle or large heavy frying pan
Jar or bowl for the curtido

ingredients.name: Red silk or black beans, canned (1 can)

steps.t: Make the curtido first so it has time to pickle: put the cabbage in a large bowl, pour over boiling water to cover, leave 1 minute and drain well. Mix with the carrot, onion, oregano, chilli flakes, vinegar, water and salt, pack into a jar or bowl and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, ideally overnight.

For the salsa, simmer the tomatoes, onion and garlic in a little water for 10 minutes until soft, then blend until smooth. Heat the oil in the saucepan, add the purée and salt and simmer for 5 minutes. It should be thin and pourable, not chunky.

For the filling, heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and soften the onion for 3 minutes. Add the beans with a splash of water and mash them to a thick paste, cooking for about 5 minutes until dry enough to hold its shape. Cool, then mix with the grated cheese.

Mix the masa harina and salt in the bowl and gradually add the warm water, mixing with your hand, then knead for 2 minutes. The dough should feel soft like modelling clay and not crack at the edges when you press a ball flat; add water a spoonful at a time if it cracks. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.

Mix a little oil and water in a small bowl to wet your hands. Roll an 80 g ball of dough, press a deep cup into it with your thumbs and fill with about 2 tablespoons of filling. Bring the edges together, pinch closed, then pat gently from hand to hand into a disc about 1 cm thick and 12 cm across. Patch any cracks.

Heat the comal over medium-high heat and brush it lightly with oil. Cook the pupusas, a few at a time, for 4–5 minutes per side, until they have brown spots, puff slightly and a little cheese oozes and crisps at the edges. Keep them warm wrapped in a tea towel while you cook the rest.
Serve hot, two per person, with a big pile of curtido and the salsa spooned over. In El Salvador they're eaten with the hands.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooked pupusas for up to 3 days or freeze for up to 2 months. Curtido keeps refrigerated for a week.
recipes.reheating: Reheat on a dry comal or frying pan over medium heat for 3–4 minutes per side, until the cheese melts again.

recipes.name: Gallo pinto (rice and beans)
recipes.description: Costa Rica's everyday breakfast: day-old rice fried with black beans and their dark cooking liquid, onion, sweet pepper and coriander until speckled like a 'spotted rooster'.

ingredients.name: Cooked white rice, preferably a day old
Cooked black beans, with 120 ml of their liquid

steps.t: Use rice cooked the day before and chilled; fresh rice turns mushy when fried. Break up any clumps with your fingers. If you're cooking beans from dried, keep some of their dark cooking liquid; it gives gallo pinto its colour.

Heat the oil in the large frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and pepper with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for about 5 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the garlic and cumin and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the beans and their liquid and simmer for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until the liquid has reduced by about half and is slightly thickened.

Tip in the rice and fold it through gently with the wooden spoon, lifting from the bottom, rather than stirring hard, so the grains stay whole. Cook for about 5 minutes, until the bean liquid is absorbed and the rice is evenly speckled and hot.
Season with Salsa Lizano, if using, and salt to taste, then fold in the coriander.
Serve hot with fried or scrambled eggs, a spoonful of natilla or soured cream, fried sweet plantains and warm corn tortillas, and a cup of strong coffee.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In Nicaragua gallo pinto is made with small red beans and the rice is fried a little longer in more oil.

recipes.name: Pastel de tres leches (three-milk cake)
recipes.description: A light sponge soaked overnight with evaporated milk, condensed milk and whole milk, then covered with softly whipped cream and a dusting of cinnamon. Cool, rich and very moist.

ingredients.name: Sweetened condensed milk (1 can, about 400 g)

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C and butter the baking dish. Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together.

Whisk the egg whites to soft peaks, then add the sugar a spoonful at a time, whisking on high until thick, glossy and holding stiff peaks. Beat in the yolks one at a time on low speed until just blended.

Gently fold in the flour mixture in three additions, alternating with the milk and vanilla, using a large spatula and cutting through the middle and turning the bowl so you keep as much air as possible. Stop as soon as no flour streaks remain.
Spread the batter in the dish and bake for 25–30 minutes, until golden, springy to the touch and a skewer in the centre comes out clean. Leave to cool for 15 minutes in the dish.

Poke holes all over the warm cake with a fork or skewer, right to the bottom. Whisk the evaporated milk, condensed milk and whole milk in the jug and pour it slowly over the cake in three or four goes, letting each lot soak in before adding more. It will look like too much liquid; the sponge absorbs it as it chills.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, until the milk has been absorbed and the cake is cold.

Before serving, whip the cold cream with the icing sugar and vanilla to soft, billowy peaks and spread it over the cake. Dust with cinnamon, cut into squares and serve cold, spooning up any milk left in the dish.

recipes.storage: @chilled

recipes.name: Ropa vieja (Cuban shredded beef)
recipes.description: Flank steak simmered until it falls into long threads, then stewed in a sofrito of onion, peppers, garlic, cumin and tomato with green olives. Served with white rice, black beans and fried plantains.
equipment: Saucepan with lid, for the rice

ingredients.name: Beef flank steak (or chuck)
ingredients.prep: cut into 3 or 4 pieces along the grain

steps.t: Put the beef in the large pot with the bay leaves, half onion and salt, and cover with about 2 litres of cold water. Bring to the boil and skim off the grey foam, then lower the heat, partly cover and simmer for 1½–2 hours, until the meat pulls apart easily with a fork.

Leave the beef to cool in its broth for 20 minutes, then lift it out and pull it apart with your fingers or two forks into long, thin shreds along the grain (the 'old clothes' of the name). Keep 250 ml of the broth.

Heat the olive oil in the deep frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and peppers and cook, stirring now and then, for 8–10 minutes, until soft and sweet. Stir in the garlic, cumin and oregano for 1 minute.

Add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute until it darkens. Pour in the wine, if using, and let it bubble for 2 minutes, then add the tomatoes and the reserved broth. Simmer for 10 minutes into a loose sauce.
Add the shredded beef and olives, stir well and simmer uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened and clings to the meat. Season with salt and pepper.
While the beef simmers, rinse the rice and cook it with 650 ml water and a pinch of salt: bring to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest for 10 minutes.
Scatter the ropa vieja with parsley and serve with the rice, Cuban black beans and fried sweet plantains (maduros).

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours (the rice within 1 hour) for up to 4 days, or freeze the beef for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Sopa de frijoles negros (Cuban black bean soup)
recipes.description: Dried black beans simmered until creamy, then enriched with a slow-cooked sofrito of onion, green pepper, garlic, cumin and oregano and sharpened with vinegar. Thick, earthy and very cheap to make.

ingredients.name: Green bell pepper (or cubanelle)
ingredients.prep: half left whole, half finely chopped

ingredients.name: Dry sherry or white wine, stirred in at the end

steps.t: Pick over the beans for small stones, rinse them and soak in plenty of cold water for 8 hours or overnight. Drain and rinse.

Put the beans in the large pot with the 2 litres of fresh water, the bay leaves and the whole half of green pepper. Bring to the boil and skim off the foam, then partly cover and simmer gently for 1½–2 hours, stirring occasionally and topping up with hot water to keep the beans covered, until they are soft and creamy inside. (A pressure cooker takes about 35 minutes.)

While the beans cook, make the sofrito: heat the olive oil in the frying pan over medium-low heat and cook the onion and chopped pepper for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until very soft and starting to turn golden. Add the garlic, cumin and oregano and stir for 1–2 minutes until fragrant.

Remove the bay leaves and the whole pepper from the beans. Scoop a ladleful of beans into the sofrito and mash them into it with a fork, then stir the whole lot back into the pot. Mashing some beans into the sofrito helps it blend in and thicken the soup.
Add the vinegar, sugar and salt and simmer uncovered for 20–30 minutes, stirring often, until the soup is thick and creamy. For a smoother soup, blend about a third of it with a stick blender.

Taste and balance with a little more vinegar or salt; it should be rich and earthy with a gentle tang. Stir in the sherry, if using. Serve hot with a drizzle of olive oil and raw chopped onion on top, and white rice on the side if you like.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Many Cuban families simmer the beans with a ham hock or bacon; this meat-free version relies on a slow sofrito for depth.

recipes.name: Mofongo
recipes.description: Puerto Rico's famous garlic plantain mash: green plantains fried until tender, then pounded in a wooden pilón with garlic, olive oil and a splash of broth and moulded into domes.
equipment: Pilón (wooden mortar and pestle) or a sturdy bowl and potato masher
Heavy pot or deep frying pan

steps.t: Peel the green plantains: cut off both ends, score the skin lengthwise along the ridges with a knife and prise it off with your thumb. Cut the plantains into 2.5 cm rounds and soak them in salted water for 10 minutes to stop them browning, then drain and pat very dry.
Make the mojo: pound the garlic and salt in the pilón to a paste, stir in the olive oil and scrape it into a small bowl.

Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 165 °C (no more than one-third full). Fry the plantains in two batches for 8–10 minutes, turning, until golden outside and tender all the way through: a knife should slide in easily. Don't let them go deep brown or they turn hard. Drain on kitchen paper.

Work quickly while the plantains are hot. Put a quarter of them in the pilón with a quarter of the garlic oil and a splash of warm stock and pound firmly into a coarse, cohesive mash with some small chunks. Add the chicharrón now, if using.
Press the mash into an oiled small bowl to shape it, then turn it out onto a plate as a dome. Repeat with the rest of the plantains.
Serve immediately, with more hot stock spooned around the base, alongside garlic prawns, roast chicken or stewed meat, or on its own with a spoon of the garlic oil.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; it firms up as it cools. Refrigerate leftovers for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered in the microwave with a splash of stock, or crumble it and fry in a little oil until crisp.

recipes.name: Curry goat
recipes.description: Bone-in goat marinated in Jamaican curry spices, thyme and scotch bonnet, browned after 'burning' the curry in hot oil and slowly stewed with potatoes until tender in a rich golden gravy.
equipment: Large heavy Dutch oven with lid
Saucepan with lid, for the rice

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.t: Rinse the goat, pat it dry and put it in the large bowl. Mix the curry spices together and rub half of them into the meat with the garlic, ginger, spring onions, thyme and salt. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight.

'Burn' the curry: heat the oil in the Dutch oven over medium heat, add the remaining curry spices and stir constantly for 1–2 minutes, until they darken slightly and smell toasty. This cooks out the raw taste of the powder; take care not to let it scorch.
Add the goat with all its marinade and turn to coat in the spiced oil. Raise the heat to medium-high and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until the meat is browned and the spices cling to it.

Add the onion, allspice berries and the whole scotch bonnet (leave it whole for flavour without fierce heat; prick it for more), then pour in the hot water. Bring to the boil, cover, lower the heat and simmer gently for 1½–2 hours, stirring occasionally and adding water if it gets dry, until the meat is tender and starting to come away from the bones.
Add the potatoes and simmer uncovered for 25–30 minutes, until they are tender and some have broken down to thicken the gravy.
Meanwhile rinse the rice and cook it with 700 ml water and a pinch of salt: bring to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest for 10 minutes.
Fish out the scotch bonnet and thyme stalks, taste the gravy and add salt. Serve the curry goat with the rice (or with rice and peas or roti) and fried plantain.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours (the rice within 1 hour) for up to 4 days, or freeze the curry for up to 3 months. It tastes even better the next day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
safety: Cook goat until browned on the outside; slow-cooked cuts are safe once tender and steaming hot throughout.

recipes.name: Doubles
recipes.description: Trinidad's beloved street breakfast: two soft, turmeric-yellow fried flatbreads (bara) piled with curried chickpeas and topped with tamarind sauce, cucumber chutney and pepper sauce.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep frying pan

steps.t: Make the bara dough: mix the flour, yeast, sugar, turmeric, cumin and salt in the large bowl. Add the warm water gradually and mix to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 2–3 minutes until smooth, rub with a little oil, cover and leave in a warm place for 1–1½ hours, until doubled.

For the channa, heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat and soften the onion for 3–4 minutes. Add the garlic and scotch bonnet for 1 minute, then the turmeric, cumin, coriander and garam masala with 2 tablespoons of water. Fry this paste, stirring, for 2 minutes until it darkens and smells toasty.

Add the chickpeas and stir to coat, then pour in the water and add the salt. Simmer for 20–25 minutes, crushing some chickpeas against the side of the pan, until they are very soft and sitting in a thick, saucy gravy. Stir in the culantro.
Make the toppings: simmer the tamarind with the brown sugar, 120 ml water and a pinch of salt for 5 minutes until syrupy. Mix the grated cucumber with the lime juice, a little culantro and salt.
Heat the frying oil to 180 °C, about 2–3 cm deep. Divide the dough into 12 balls. With oiled hands, flatten each on an oiled surface into a thin 10–12 cm round.
Fry the bara one or two at a time for 15–20 seconds per side, until puffed and very lightly golden; they should stay soft and pliable, not crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and stack in a tea towel.

To serve, overlap two bara, spoon a generous amount of channa on top and add tamarind sauce, cucumber chutney and pepper sauce to taste. Fold the bara over and eat straight away; doubles are meant to be messy.

recipes.storage: Bara is best fresh. Keep the channa refrigerated for up to 4 days and the tamarind sauce for 2 weeks.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the channa until steaming; warm bara briefly in a dry pan or wrapped in foil in a low oven.

recipes.name: Ajiaco santafereño (Bogotá chicken and potato soup)
recipes.description: Bogotá's signature soup of chicken, corn on the cob and three kinds of potato, one of which melts to thicken the broth, flavoured with the herb guascas and served with cream, capers and avocado.

ingredients.name: Floury white potatoes (papa sabanera or russet)
All-purpose potatoes (papa pastusa or Yukon Gold)
Papa criolla (small yellow potatoes) or baby waxy potatoes

steps.t: Put the chicken, stock, water, spring onions, garlic, coriander stems and salt in the large pot. Bring to the boil, skim off the foam, then simmer gently for 25–30 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (74 °C in the thickest part). Lift out the chicken and strain the broth back into the pot.
Add the sliced floury potatoes and the all-purpose potatoes to the broth and simmer for 20 minutes. The floury ones will start to fall apart; that's what thickens ajiaco.

Add the corn and the papas criollas and simmer for 25–30 minutes more, stirring now and then so nothing sticks, until the criollas have softened and partly collapsed and the soup is thick, creamy and pale yellow. Mash some of the potatoes against the side of the pot if it needs more body.
Meanwhile, pull the chicken into bite-sized shreds, discarding any skin and bones.

Return the chicken to the pot with the guascas and pepper and simmer for 5–10 minutes. Adding the guascas near the end keeps their grassy, slightly artichoke-like aroma. Taste and adjust the salt; the soup should be thick like a stew.
Ladle into deep bowls, making sure each has a piece of corn. Bring the cream, capers and avocado to the table so everyone can add their own, with white rice on the side if you like.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 3 days; it thickens as it cools, so thin it with water when reheating. Don't freeze: the potatoes go grainy.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Guascas (Galinsoga parviflora) are sold dried in Latin American shops. Without them the soup is still good but less distinctive; don't substitute another strong herb.
Papa criolla is a small, buttery Andean yellow potato that dissolves when cooked; waxy yellow potatoes are the nearest substitute.

recipes.name: Empanadas de carne (Argentinian beef empanadas)
recipes.description: Baked half-moon pastries filled with hand-cut beef, sweet onion, spring onion, paprika and cumin with egg and olive, closed with the traditional twisted repulgue edge. Two or three make a meal.

ingredients.name: Beef rump or sirloin
ingredients.prep: cut by hand into 5 mm dice

steps.t: Make the filling at least 2 hours ahead, or the day before. Heat the oil in the large frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions and pepper for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until very soft and sweet but not browned. Stir in the paprika, cumin, chilli and oregano for 30 seconds.

Turn the heat up, add the diced beef and salt and cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until the meat is no longer red on the outside; it finishes cooking in the oven and stays juicy. Take off the heat, stir in the spring onions and taste: it should be boldly seasoned. Cool, then chill until cold and firm.

Make the dough: mix the flour and salt in the bowl, pour in the melted butter and rub it in with your fingertips. Add the warm water gradually and knead for 5–7 minutes, until smooth, soft and elastic. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes so it rolls without shrinking back.
Roll the dough out thinly, about 3 mm, and cut 13–14 cm circles, re-rolling the scraps; you should get about 18. Keep them covered so they don't dry out.

Put 2 tablespoons of cold filling on each circle with a little chopped egg and half an olive. Brush the edge with water, fold over into a half-moon and press to seal. Make the repulgue: starting at one corner, fold a small piece of the edge over itself and pinch, then repeat all the way round to form a rope. If that's tricky, crimp firmly with a fork.

Heat the oven to 220 °C. Set the empanadas on lined trays, brush them with beaten egg and bake for 15–20 minutes, until golden brown with darker spots. A little juice bubbling at the seams is a good sign.
Rest them for 5 minutes, as the filling is very hot and juicy. Serve warm with lemon wedges to squeeze inside, as they do in Tucumán, and a green salad.

recipes.storage: Freeze unbaked empanadas on a tray, then bag them, for up to 3 months; bake from frozen, adding 5 minutes. Baked ones keep refrigerated for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for about 10 minutes until hot through.
notes: Ready-made empanada discs (tapas para empanadas) work well if you're short of time.
Tucumán cooks also fry them in beef fat; Mendoza's version adds raisins, and Salta's includes diced potato.

recipes.name: Empanadas colombianas (corn empanadas with beef and potato)
recipes.description: Crisp, golden yellow-corn empanadas filled with beef and potato cooked in hogao, a slow tomato and spring onion sauce, fried and served with tangy ají picante and lime.

ingredients.name: Limes
ingredients.prep: 1 juiced for the ají, 1 in wedges

steps.t: Boil the potatoes in salted water for 15–18 minutes until very tender, drain and mash roughly, leaving a few small lumps.

Make the hogao: heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the spring onions and onion for 3 minutes. Add the garlic, grated tomato, cumin, achiote and a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for about 10 minutes, until thick and jammy.

Add the beef to the hogao, breaking it up, and cook for 6–8 minutes until no pink remains. Mix in the mashed potato and salt; the filling should taste slightly over-seasoned because the corn dough is mild. Let it cool completely.
Make the ají: mix the coriander, spring onions, chilli, vinegar, water, the juice of one lime and a pinch of salt. Leave it for at least 15 minutes for the flavours to blend.

For the dough, mix the masarepa, salt and achiote, then add the warm water gradually and knead for 2–3 minutes into a smooth, soft dough that doesn't crack when pressed. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.

Cut open a zip bag along the sides to make a folding plastic sheet. Put a 40 g ball of dough inside and press it with a plate to a thin round about 12 cm across. Put a heaped tablespoon of filling on one half, fold the plastic over to close the empanada, press the edges together, then press a small bowl over it to cut a neat half-moon. Peel off the plastic and repeat.

Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 180 °C (no more than one-third full). Fry the empanadas 3 or 4 at a time for 3–4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper. Serve hot with the ají spooned into each bite and lime wedges.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked empanadas on a tray, then bag, for up to 3 months and fry from frozen (add 1–2 minutes). Refrigerate fried ones for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes.

recipes.name: Arepas reina pepiada (chicken-avocado arepas)
recipes.description: Crisp-crusted Venezuelan corn arepas split open and stuffed with reina pepiada: shredded chicken folded into a creamy, lime-sharp avocado and mayonnaise salad with onion and coriander.

ingredients.name: White precooked cornmeal (masarepa, such as Harina P.A.N.)

steps.t: Put the chicken in the saucepan with the onion piece, garlic clove and a good pinch of salt, cover with cold water and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15–18 minutes, until the thickest part reaches 74 °C. Leave it in the liquid for 10 minutes, then shred it very finely with two forks.

Mash the avocado in the bowl with the lime juice, grated garlic and mayonnaise until creamy. Fold in the shredded chicken, onion, coriander, salt and pepper. Taste and add more lime or salt; it should be creamy and bright. Press cling film onto the surface and chill while you make the arepas.

Pour the warm water into a bowl and stir in the salt. Add the masarepa gradually, mixing with your hand, then knead for about 2 minutes until smooth and soft. The dough should not stick to your hands or crack at the edges when you press a ball flat; add a spoonful of water or masarepa to adjust. Rest it for 5 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls of about 85 g. Flatten each between your palms into a disc 1.5 cm thick and 9–10 cm across, smoothing any cracks at the edge with damp fingers.

Heat the pan over medium heat and brush it with oil. Cook the arepas for 6–8 minutes per side, turning once, until they have a crisp crust with brown spots and sound hollow when tapped. For puffier arepas, finish them in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes.
While the arepas are hot, split each one open with the serrated knife about three-quarters of the way round to make a pocket. Stuff generously with the reina pepiada and serve straight away.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the filling with cling film pressed onto it for up to 2 days. Cooked arepas keep refrigerated for 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat arepas in a dry pan or a 180 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until crisp; the filling is served cold.

recipes.name: Arepa de huevo (egg-stuffed fried arepa)
recipes.description: A Caribbean-coast breakfast and beach snack: a yellow corn arepa fried until it puffs, slit open, filled with a raw egg, sealed and fried again until the egg is set inside a crisp shell.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep frying pan

ingredients.name: Ají or hot sauce, to serve

steps.t: Mix the masarepa, salt and sugar in the bowl, add the warm water gradually and knead for 2–3 minutes into a smooth, soft dough. Keep back a walnut-sized piece for sealing. Divide the rest into 6 balls and cover them with a damp cloth.
Put each ball between two sheets of plastic and press it with a plate into a disc about 12–13 cm across and 5 mm thick. Keep the edges even; thin spots tear when you open the pocket.

Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 175 °C, about 5 cm deep. Fry the discs one or two at a time for 2–3 minutes, turning once, until they puff up like pillows and turn pale golden. If one doesn't puff, it can still be opened carefully. Drain on kitchen paper.

Hold each puffed arepa upright in a tea towel and cut a 4–5 cm slit along the edge with the small knife, opening a pocket inside without cutting through the other side. Crack an egg into the small cup, season it with a pinch of salt and pour it into the pocket.
Seal the opening by pressing a small piece of the reserved dough over it, smoothing the edges. Work over a plate in case of leaks.

Slide the filled arepas back into the oil, sealed side down, and fry for 2–3 minutes, then turn and fry for 2–3 minutes more, until deep golden and crisp and the egg feels firm when pressed (the white must be fully set). Drain and serve hot with ají or hot sauce.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly fried; they don't keep well once filled. Unfilled fried discs can be refrigerated for a day.
notes: On the coast many cooks add a spoonful of cooked minced beef to the pocket with the egg.

recipes.name: Pabellón criollo
recipes.description: Venezuela's national plate: shredded beef stewed in sofrito, black beans with a touch of sweetness, white rice and caramelised fried ripe plantain, served side by side.

steps.t: Drain the soaked beans, cover them with 1.5 litres of fresh water in a large pot and simmer, partly covered, for 1½–2 hours, until creamy-tender, topping up with hot water as needed. At the same time, put the beef in the other pot with the bay leaves and water to cover, bring to the boil, skim and simmer for 1½–2 hours until it shreds easily. Keep 250 ml of the beef broth.

Shred the cooled beef finely with your fingers or two forks. Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion and red pepper for 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cumin for 1 minute, then the tomatoes for 5 minutes until broken down.
Add the beef, Worcestershire sauce, salt and the reserved broth and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until juicy but no longer soupy. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

Finish the beans: soften the onion, green pepper and garlic in 2 tablespoons of oil for 5 minutes, add the cumin, then stir this into the beans with the sugar and salt. Simmer uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring and mashing a few beans, until thick with only a little sauce.

Make the rice: heat the oil in the saucepan, add the garlic and rinsed rice and stir for 2 minutes until the grains turn opaque. Add 600 ml water and a pinch of salt, bring to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 18 minutes, then rest for 10 minutes and remove the garlic.

Peel the plantains and cut them diagonally into long slices 1 cm thick. Heat the oil in a clean frying pan over medium heat and fry the slices for 3 minutes per side, until deep golden and caramelised at the edges. Drain on kitchen paper.
Serve each plate with the rice, beans and beef side by side, like the stripes of a flag, with the tajadas on top or alongside. Add a fried egg on top to make it 'a caballo'.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate each component separately within 2 hours (the rice within 1 hour) for up to 3 days; the beef and beans freeze well for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Cachapas (sweet corn pancakes with cheese)
