recipes.description: Thick, slightly sweet pancakes made from blended fresh corn, cooked on a griddle until lacy and brown and folded around slices of soft white cheese that melt in the heat.
equipment: Large non-stick frying pan or griddle

ingredients.name: Sweetcorn kernels, fresh or frozen and thawed
Precooked cornmeal (masarepa)
ingredients.prep: only if the batter is thin

ingredients.name: Butter
ingredients.prep: for the pan and to serve

ingredients.name: Queso de mano or fresh mozzarella

steps.t: Put the corn, milk, egg, sugar and salt in the blender and blend to a thick, slightly coarse batter, like a heavy pancake batter with tiny bits of corn. Scrape down the sides once or twice.
Check the consistency: it should pour slowly from a spoon. If it's runny (frozen corn can be watery), stir in the masarepa a tablespoon at a time and leave it for 5 minutes to thicken.
Heat the frying pan over medium heat and grease it with a little butter. Pour in about 150 ml of batter and spread it gently into a round about 15 cm across and 5 mm thick.

Cook for 3–4 minutes, until bubbles appear, the edges look dry and the underside is golden with darker brown spots; the natural corn sugars brown quickly, so lower the heat if it colours too fast. Flip carefully with a wide spatula and cook for 2–3 minutes more.

Lay slices of cheese over half of the cachapa while it is still in the pan, fold the other half over and leave for 30 seconds so the cheese starts to melt. Slide onto a plate, top with a little butter and keep warm while you cook the rest.
Serve hot, as they do at roadside stands, with more butter, a fried egg or shredded beef (carne mechada) on the side and a cup of strong coffee.

recipes.storage: Best fresh. Refrigerate cooked cachapas without the cheese for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a dry pan for 2 minutes per side, then add the cheese and fold.

recipes.name: Locro de papa (Ecuadorian potato and cheese soup)
recipes.description: A thick, golden Andean potato soup coloured with achiote and enriched with milk and fresh cheese, topped with avocado. Comfort food from the highlands around Quito.

ingredients.name: Spring onions
ingredients.prep: whites chopped, greens sliced for garnish

ingredients.name: Floury and waxy potatoes, mixed
ingredients.prep: peeled; half cut into 2 cm cubes, half grated or sliced thinly

ingredients.name: Queso fresco
ingredients.prep: cut into small cubes, to serve

steps.t: Melt the butter in the large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and spring onion whites and cook gently for 5–6 minutes, until soft and translucent. Stir in the garlic, cumin and achiote and cook for 1 minute until fragrant and the butter turns orange.
Add all the potatoes and stir for 2 minutes to coat them in the spiced butter. The thinly sliced or grated portion will dissolve and thicken the soup; the cubes keep their shape.
Pour in the water or stock, add the salt and bring to the boil. Lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 25–30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are very soft.
Mash about half of the potatoes in the pot with the masher, leaving plenty of chunks, until the soup is thick and creamy.

Pour in the milk and bring back to a gentle simmer for 5 minutes, stirring. Don't let it boil hard, or the milk can catch and the cheese turn stringy. Take off the heat and stir in the crumbled cheese until it softens. Taste for salt.
Ladle into bowls and top each with cubes of fresh cheese, avocado slices, coriander and spring onion greens. In Ecuador it's often served with ají (chilli sauce) on the side.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, stirring and adding a splash of milk or water; don't boil hard or the cheese turns stringy.

recipes.name: Ceviche de pescado (Peruvian fish ceviche)
recipes.description: Lima-style ceviche: cubes of very fresh white fish 'cooked' for just a few minutes in lime juice with chilli, garlic and red onion, served in its leche de tigre with sweet potato and corn.

ingredients.name: Very fresh, sashimi-grade white fish (corvina, sea bass, sole or flounder)
Ají limo or other hot chilli (or ½ habanero)
Freshly squeezed lime juice (from about 12 small limes)
Orange sweet potato
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm rounds

steps.t: Cook the sides first so they can cool: simmer the sweet potato rounds in salted water for 15–20 minutes until tender, and boil the corn in another pan for 8–10 minutes. Drain and leave at room temperature.
Slice the red onion as thinly as possible along the grain, soak it in iced water for 10 minutes to make it crisp and milder, then drain and pat dry.

Keep the fish very cold. Cut it into 2 cm cubes and put them in the chilled bowl. Sprinkle with the salt, chilli, garlic and ginger and stir for about 1 minute; the salt draws out a little protein, which helps the lime work quickly and makes the leche de tigre creamy.

Squeeze the limes gently, by hand or with a light squeezer: pressing too hard releases bitter oils from the pith. Pour the juice over the fish so it is just covered and stir with a spoon for 1–2 minutes.

Leave for 2–5 minutes only, in the Lima style: the outside of each cube turns white and opaque while the centre stays translucent and tender. Fold in the onion and coriander, then taste the juice; it should be sharp, salty and spicy. Adjust with salt or chilli.

Serve immediately in chilled bowls with plenty of the leche de tigre (the citrus juice) spooned over, with sweet potato, corn and a lettuce leaf on the side. Ceviche waits for no one: the lime keeps 'cooking' the fish and turns it rubbery.

recipes.storage: Ceviche must be eaten as soon as it's made; don't keep leftovers.
notes: Use fish sold for raw eating (previously frozen), bought on the day; ask the fishmonger for sashimi grade.

recipes.name: Lomo saltado
recipes.description: A Chinese-Peruvian wok stir-fry of beef strips, red onion, tomato and ají amarillo flashed with soy sauce and vinegar, tossed with crisp chips and served with white rice.
equipment: Wok or large heavy frying pan

ingredients.name: Ají amarillo (or a mild yellow chilli)

steps.t: Start the rice: rinse it, then cook with 500 ml water, a pinch of salt and a little oil: bring to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then rest for 10. Soak the chips in cold water while you prepare everything else, then dry them very well.

Heat the frying oil to 160 °C and fry the chips in batches for 5–6 minutes until soft and pale. Raise the oil to 190 °C and fry them again for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain, salt and keep warm in a low oven.
Toss the beef with the cumin, garlic, pepper and salt. Mix the soy sauce and vinegar in a cup. Have the onion, tomato, chilli and coriander ready by the stove: the stir-fry takes only a few minutes.

Heat the wok over the highest heat until it smokes. Add 1 tablespoon of oil and half the beef in a single layer and leave it for 1 minute to sear, then toss for 30 seconds; it should be browned outside and still pink inside. Tip onto a plate and repeat with the rest.

Add the remaining oil to the wok, then the onion, and toss over high heat for about 1 minute until charred at the edges but still crunchy. Add the chilli and tomatoes and toss for 30 seconds, just until warmed. If using pisco, add it now and carefully tilt the wok to flame it.

Return the beef and its juices, pour the soy-vinegar mixture around the hot sides of the wok so it sizzles and caramelises, and toss everything for 30 seconds. Turn off the heat and toss in the coriander and half the chips so they soak up some of the juices.
Serve straight away with the rice and the rest of the chips on the side or on top. The juices that pool on the plate are meant to be mopped up with rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately. Refrigerate leftover beef and vegetables for up to 2 days (the chips go soft).
recipes.reheating: Reheat the beef and vegetables quickly in a very hot pan; re-crisp the chips in a hot oven.

recipes.name: Ají de gallina (creamy chilli chicken)
recipes.description: Shredded chicken in a velvety yellow sauce of ají amarillo, onion, bread soaked in evaporated milk, walnuts and Parmesan, served over potatoes with rice, egg and black olives.
equipment: Saucepans for the potatoes, rice and eggs

steps.t: Put the chicken, carrot, celery, half onion and salt in the large saucepan with 1.2 litres of water. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 15–20 minutes, until the chicken reaches 74 °C in the thickest part. Leave it to cool in the broth, then shred it finely by hand. Strain and keep 500 ml of the broth.
Tear the bread into the blender jug, pour over the evaporated milk and leave to soak for 10 minutes. Add the walnuts and blend to a smooth, thick cream.
Meanwhile, boil the potatoes, cook the rice (rinsed, with 650 ml water, covered on low heat for 15 minutes then rested for 10) and hard-boil the eggs for 10 minutes, then cool them in cold water.

Make the aderezo, the flavour base: heat the oil in the wide pan over medium-low heat and cook the chopped onion for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until very soft and translucent but not browned. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the ají amarillo paste, cumin and turmeric, and cook for 3–4 minutes until fragrant and the oil turns golden.

Stir in the bread cream, then add the reserved broth a ladle at a time, stirring constantly, until the sauce is thick, smooth and creamy, like a pouring custard. Simmer gently for 5–8 minutes, stirring so it doesn't catch.
Add the shredded chicken and Parmesan and simmer for 5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper; add a splash more broth if it is too stiff. It should be creamy and coat the chicken generously.
Lay slices of potato on each plate, spoon the ají de gallina over them and serve with a mound of rice, half an egg and two olives on top.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of broth or milk, stirring, until steaming hot.

recipes.name: Causa limeña (layered potato terrine)
recipes.description: A cold Lima classic: smooth yellow potato seasoned with lime and ají amarillo, layered with creamy chicken salad and avocado, then sliced and topped with egg and olives.
equipment: 20 cm square dish or ring mould

steps.t: Boil the whole, unpeeled potatoes in salted water for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides in easily. Peel them while still warm and press them through the ricer or a sieve into a bowl. Lumps won't smooth out later, so rice them while hot.

Let the potato cool until just warm, then add the ají amarillo paste, lime juice, oil and salt and knead it with your hands until smooth, bright yellow and pliable like modelling clay. Taste: it should be tangy, salty and gently spicy.

While the potatoes cook, poach the chicken in lightly salted simmering water for 15 minutes, until it reaches 74 °C. Cool, shred finely and mix with the mayonnaise, onion, lime juice and a pinch of salt.

Line the dish with cling film, leaving some overhanging. Press half the potato evenly into the base, about 1.5 cm thick. Spread the chicken over it, then lay the avocado slices on top in an even layer and season them with a pinch of salt.
Cover with the remaining potato and smooth the top with a wet spatula. Fold the cling film over and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, until firm enough to slice.

Lift the causa out using the cling film, cut it into squares with a knife dipped in hot water and top each with a dot of mayonnaise, a slice of egg, an olive half and a little parsley. Serve cold as a light lunch or a starter.

recipes.storage: Keep chilled and eat within 2 days; the avocado darkens a little over time.
notes: Tuna (two 160 g cans, drained) mixed with mayonnaise is an equally traditional filling.

recipes.name: Papa a la huancaína (potatoes in spicy cheese sauce)
recipes.description: Boiled yellow potatoes blanketed in huancaína, a creamy, pale-gold sauce of fresh cheese, evaporated milk and ají amarillo, garnished with egg and black olives.

steps.t: Put the potatoes in the saucepan, cover with cold salted water and boil for 18–20 minutes until tender. At the same time, boil the eggs in the small saucepan for 10 minutes, then cool them in cold water and peel.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion, garlic and ají amarillo paste for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until soft and fragrant. This takes the raw edge off the onion and deepens the chilli flavour.

Blend the cooked onion mixture with the cheese, evaporated milk, remaining oil and salt until completely smooth and thick, like double cream. Add a splash more milk if it's too thick to pour, and taste for salt and heat.
Peel the potatoes if you like and cut them into thick slices. Lay the lettuce leaves on a platter, arrange the potatoes on top and pour over plenty of sauce.
Garnish with egg halves and olives and serve at room temperature as a starter or side, or with grilled meat. The sauce is also excellent as a dip.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the sauce in a covered container for up to 3 days (it thickens; loosen with milk). Keep the potatoes separately.
notes: Many Peruvian cooks blend in 2–4 soda crackers to thicken the sauce.

recipes.name: Salteñas (Bolivian juicy baked empanadas)
recipes.description: Bolivia's mid-morning treat: slightly sweet golden pastry wrapped around a spicy beef, potato and pea stew set with gelatine, which melts in the oven into a juicy broth you sip as you eat.
equipment: Shallow dish for chilling the filling

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled, cut into 1 cm dice and boiled until just tender

ingredients.name: Egg
ingredients.prep: beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for glazing

steps.t: Make the jigote the day before, or at least 5 hours ahead. Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10 minutes until soft. Stir in the paprika, chilli powder, cumin, oregano and sugar for 2 minutes, then add the beef and cook for 5 minutes, until it is no longer red outside.

Pour in 380 ml of the stock, add the salt and simmer for 15 minutes, until the beef is tender. Add the diced potato and peas and simmer for 5 minutes more. The stew should be very juicy and boldly seasoned, slightly sweet and spicy.

Sprinkle the gelatine over the remaining 120 ml of cold stock and leave it to swell for 5 minutes. Take the stew off the heat, stir in the gelatine until dissolved, then add the spring onions and parsley. Pour into the shallow dish, cool and refrigerate until set firm, at least 4 hours. This is the secret of a juicy salteña: the filling must be solid when you wrap it.

Make the dough: mix the flour, sugar, salt and achiote in the bowl. Pour in the hot melted butter and rub it in with your fingertips, then add the beaten egg and enough warm water to make a soft dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth and slightly oily, cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 12 balls and roll each into a 14–15 cm circle about 3 mm thick. Put 3 tablespoons of cold, set jigote in the centre with a piece of egg, an olive and a few raisins. Brush the edge with water, bring the sides up over the filling and press firmly to seal along the top.

Stand the salteñas upright with the seam on top and crimp it into a tight braid by folding and pinching along its length; any gap will leak. Chill them for 20 minutes while the oven heats to 220 °C. Brush with the egg glaze.
Bake upright on the lined tray for 18–22 minutes, until deep golden-orange. The jelly melts back into a hot broth inside.
Rest for 5 minutes, then eat upright: bite off a corner, sip the juice and eat your way down, ideally mid-morning as Bolivians do.

recipes.storage: Freeze unbaked salteñas for up to 2 months and bake from frozen (add 5–8 minutes). Baked ones keep refrigerated for 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 10–12 minutes until the filling is liquid and steaming.

recipes.name: Sopa de maní (Bolivian peanut soup)
recipes.description: A creamy Bolivian soup of blended raw peanuts simmered in beef broth with vegetables, potatoes and small pasta, topped with crisp shoestring potatoes and parsley.

ingredients.name: Beef shin or chuck, on the bone if possible
Potato
ingredients.prep: cut into thin matchsticks, for frying

steps.t: Put the beef in the large pot with the 2.5 litres of water and the salt. Bring to the boil, skim off the foam, then simmer gently, partly covered, for about 1 hour, until the meat is tender. This makes the broth.
Blend the raw peanuts with the 500 ml of water for 2–3 minutes, until you have a completely smooth peanut milk. For an extra-silky soup, strain it through a sieve.
Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion, pepper and carrot for 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, cumin and oregano and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Stir the vegetables and the peanut milk into the broth. Bring it back to the boil slowly, stirring constantly: peanut milk foams up and sticks to the bottom easily. Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring often.

Add the diced potatoes and pasta and simmer for 12–15 minutes, until both are tender; add the peas for the last 5 minutes. The soup should be creamy and pale; add hot water if it gets too thick. Taste for salt.

While the soup finishes, heat the frying oil to 180 °C in the small pot, dry the potato matchsticks well and fry them in batches for 3–4 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and salt.
Serve the soup with a piece of beef in each bowl, topped with a handful of crisp potato sticks and parsley. Bolivians add llajwa (fresh tomato and chilli salsa) at the table.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, stirring and adding water as it thickens; the pasta softens on standing, so add the fried potatoes only when serving.

recipes.name: Moqueca baiana (Bahian fish and coconut stew)
recipes.description: Firm fish gently stewed between layers of onion, peppers and tomato in coconut milk and red dendê palm oil, finished with coriander and lime. Served from the pot with white rice.
equipment: Wide clay pot or heavy casserole with a lid
Saucepan with lid, for the rice

ingredients.name: Firm white fish steaks or chunks (snapper, grouper, sea bass or cod)

steps.t: Put the fish in the bowl with the lime juice, garlic, salt and pepper and turn to coat. Cover and refrigerate for 20–30 minutes; the lime seasons and firms the fish slightly.
While it marinates, start the rice: rinse it and cook with 500 ml water and a pinch of salt, covered on the lowest heat, for 15 minutes, then rest for 10 minutes off the heat.

Drizzle the olive oil over the base of the clay pot and lay in half the onion, peppers and tomatoes. Arrange the fish on top with its marinade, then cover with the rest of the vegetables, half the coriander, the spring onions and the chilli.
Pour the coconut milk over everything and drizzle the dendê on top. Cover and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then cook for 10 minutes without stirring.

Uncover, gently shake the pot or spoon the sauce over the fish, and cook for 5–8 minutes more, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily and the sauce is a rich orange. Don't stir hard or the fish will break up.
Taste the sauce and add salt or a squeeze of lime. Scatter with the remaining coriander and bring the pot to the table. Serve with the white rice, and with pirão or farofa if you have them.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, covered, over low heat until steaming, without boiling hard.
notes: Dendê gives moqueca baiana its colour and flavour. The Capixaba moqueca from Espírito Santo leaves out dendê and coconut milk and uses olive oil and annatto instead.

recipes.name: Coxinha (Brazilian chicken croquettes)
recipes.description: Brazil's favourite party and snack-bar savoury: a smooth dough cooked in chicken broth, wrapped around creamy shredded chicken into teardrop shapes, crumbed and fried until golden.

steps.t: Put the chicken in the large saucepan with the onion half, bay leaf, a good pinch of salt and 1 litre of water. Simmer gently for 15–18 minutes, until the chicken reaches 74 °C. Lift it out, shred it finely and strain the broth; measure 750 ml for the dough, topping up with water if needed.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the chopped onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and tomato paste for 1 minute, then the shredded chicken, salt and pepper, and cook for 3 minutes. Take off the heat, stir in the parsley and spring onions and leave to cool, then mix in the cream cheese.

Make the dough: bring the measured broth, butter and salt to the boil in the heavy saucepan. Tip in all the flour at once and stir hard with the wooden spoon over low heat for 2–3 minutes, until it comes together into a smooth ball that pulls away from the sides of the pan, much like choux pastry.

Turn the dough onto an oiled worktop. As soon as it's cool enough to handle, knead it for 3–5 minutes until completely smooth and silky; this prevents cracks when shaping. Keep it covered with a bowl.

With lightly oiled hands, take a 40 g piece of dough, flatten it into a cup in your palm and fill it with a heaped tablespoon of filling. Close the dough around it, pinching the top into a point to make a teardrop (the 'little thigh' of the name) with a flat base. Repeat to make about 24.
Dip each coxinha in the beaten egg, then roll it in the breadcrumbs until evenly coated. Chill for 20 minutes so the coating sets and they hold their shape in the oil.

Heat the oil in the heavy pot to 175–180 °C (no more than one-third full). Fry 4 or 5 at a time for 4–5 minutes, turning, until deep golden all over. Drain on kitchen paper and serve hot, with hot sauce or a squeeze of lime.

recipes.storage: Freeze shaped, crumbed coxinhas on a tray, then bag them, for up to 3 months; fry from frozen at 170 °C. Refrigerate fried ones for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven or air fryer for 8–10 minutes until hot through.

recipes.name: Brigadeiros (chocolate fudge balls)
recipes.description: Brazil's essential party sweet: condensed milk, cocoa and butter stirred into a glossy fudge, rolled into small balls and coated in chocolate sprinkles. Soft, chewy and very chocolatey.

ingredients.name: Sweetened condensed milk (1 can, about 400 g)
Butter
ingredients.prep: plus a little for your hands

steps.t: Butter a large plate and set out the mini paper cases and a shallow bowl of chocolate sprinkles before you start, because the hot fudge needs to come off the heat as soon as it's ready.
Put the condensed milk, cocoa, butter and salt in the saucepan and stir over medium-low heat until the cocoa has dissolved and the mixture is smooth.

Keep cooking, stirring constantly and scraping the base and corners with the spatula, for 10–15 minutes. It will bubble, thicken and darken. It's ready when you can draw the spatula across the bottom of the pan and the line stays open for 2–3 seconds, and the mass slides away from the pan in one piece.
Scrape the mixture onto the buttered plate, spread it out a little and leave to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate for about 1 hour, until firm enough to shape.
Butter your hands lightly and roll teaspoons of the mixture (about 15 g each) into smooth balls. Roll each one in the chocolate sprinkles until completely covered and set it in a paper case.
Serve at room temperature, when they're soft and chewy. For brigadeiro de colher, stop cooking a few minutes earlier and eat it warm with a spoon.

recipes.storage: Keep covered at room temperature for 1 day or refrigerated for up to 5 days; bring back to room temperature before serving.

recipes.name: Pão de queijo (Brazilian cheese bread)
recipes.description: Little cheese breads from Minas Gerais made with tapioca starch: crisp outside, chewy and stretchy inside, with a savoury tang of cheese. Naturally gluten-free.

ingredients.name: Tapioca starch (polvilho doce, or half polvilho azedo)

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C and line the baking tray with baking paper. Put the tapioca starch in the large bowl.

Bring the milk, water, oil and salt to the boil in the saucepan, then pour it straight over the starch and stir hard with the wooden spoon. It will look lumpy and gluey; scalding the starch like this gelatinises it and gives pão de queijo its chewy texture.

Leave the dough for 10–15 minutes until warm rather than hot, so the eggs don't scramble. Add the egg a little at a time, beating or kneading with your hand after each addition, until the dough is smooth, sticky and stretchy.

Add both cheeses and knead them in until evenly mixed. The dough should be soft and hold its shape when rolled; if it's too loose to roll, add a spoonful of starch, and if it's dry and crumbly, a splash of milk.
Oil your hands and roll the dough into balls about 3 cm across (about 25 g each). Set them 3 cm apart on the tray.

Bake for 20–25 minutes, until puffed, cracked on top and golden at the base; don't open the oven for the first 15 minutes or they may collapse. Serve warm, with coffee, as they soften and deflate slightly as they cool.

recipes.storage: Freeze unbaked balls on a tray, then bag them, for up to 3 months; bake from frozen at 180 °C for 25–30 minutes. Baked ones are best the same day.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 180 °C oven for 5 minutes.

recipes.name: Chimichurri
recipes.description: Argentina's sauce for the asado: hand-chopped parsley, garlic, oregano and chilli flakes in red wine vinegar and oil, spooned over grilled beef, sausages, provoleta and bread.

ingredients.name: Flat-leaf parsley (1 large bunch)
ingredients.prep: leaves and tender stems, finely chopped

steps.t: Dissolve the salt in the hot water to make a salmuera (brine) and leave it to cool. The brine seasons the sauce evenly and helps the dried oregano soften.
Chop the parsley finely by hand with a sharp knife rather than in a food processor, which bruises it into a bitter paste. Mince the garlic very finely.

Put the parsley, garlic, oregano, chilli flakes, pepper and paprika, if using, in the jar. Pour in the cooled brine and the vinegar and stir, then add the oil and stir again. The herbs should be loosely covered with liquid.

Leave the chimichurri for at least 30 minutes, and ideally 2 hours or overnight, so the oregano rehydrates and the flavours come together. Stir and taste before serving; add more vinegar for tang or chilli for heat.
Spoon it generously over grilled or barbecued beef, chorizo, chicken, provoleta or grilled vegetables, or onto crusty bread.

recipes.storage: Keep in a covered jar in the fridge, topped with a little oil, for up to 1 week; bring to room temperature before serving.

recipes.name: Milanesa de carne (breaded beef cutlet)
recipes.description: Thin slices of beef soaked in garlicky, parsley-flecked egg, pressed into breadcrumbs and shallow-fried until crisp and golden. Argentina's everyday favourite, served with lemon.

ingredients.name: Beef topside or rump (nalga or bola de lomo)

steps.t: Lay the beef slices between two sheets of cling film and pound them with the mallet to an even 5 mm thickness. Snip the edges in two or three places so they don't curl in the pan.

Beat the eggs in a shallow dish with the garlic, parsley, salt and pepper. Add the beef and turn to coat. Argentines often leave the meat in the egg for 15 minutes or overnight in the fridge, which gives a more flavourful, tender milanesa.

Spread the breadcrumbs in the second dish. Lift each slice from the egg, let the excess drip off, and press it firmly into the crumbs on both sides so they stick in an even layer. For a thicker crust, dip it in egg and crumbs a second time.

Heat 1 cm of oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat to about 175 °C; a crumb dropped in should sizzle immediately. Fry the milanesas one or two at a time for 2–3 minutes per side, until deep golden and crisp. The thin beef is cooked through by the time the crust is golden.
Drain on the wire rack (kitchen paper underneath makes the base soggy) and keep warm in a low oven while you fry the rest.
Serve straight away with lemon wedges and mashed potato, chips or a simple salad. For milanesa a la napolitana, top with tomato sauce and mozzarella and grill until bubbling.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes; cold milanesa also makes a classic sandwich.

recipes.name: Pastel de choclo (Chilean corn and beef pie)
recipes.description: A Chilean summer classic: spiced beef and onion pino with chicken, egg, olives and raisins, covered with a basil-scented fresh corn purée and baked until the sugared top caramelises.
equipment: 6 individual clay dishes or a 23 × 33 cm baking dish

steps.t: Make the pino: heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until very soft and translucent. Stir in the paprika, cumin and oregano for 1 minute.

Add the beef, breaking it up, and cook for 8 minutes until browned with no pink remaining. Sprinkle in the flour, stir for 1 minute, then add the stock and salt and simmer for 5 minutes. The pino should be juicy but not wet. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

Season the chicken with salt and brown it in a little oil in a frying pan for 4 minutes per side. Add a splash of water, cover and cook for 10 minutes more, until it reaches 74 °C. Cut it into bite-sized pieces.

Make the pastelera: blend the corn with the milk to a coarse purée. Melt the butter in the heavy saucepan over medium heat, add the corn, basil and salt and cook, stirring constantly, for 10–15 minutes, until it thickens like soft polenta and a spoon drawn through it leaves a trail. It sticks easily, so keep stirring.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Spread the pino in the dishes, then add the chicken pieces, egg quarters, olives and raisins.
Spoon the corn over the filling and smooth it to cover completely. Sprinkle evenly with the sugar.

Bake for 25–30 minutes, until bubbling at the edges, then finish under a hot grill for 3–5 minutes, watching closely, until the top is golden with caramelised brown spots. Rest for 10 minutes and serve with ensalada chilena.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered in a 180 °C oven for 20–25 minutes until steaming in the centre.

recipes.name: Empanadas de pino (Chilean baked beef empanadas)
recipes.description: Large baked Chilean empanadas, the centrepiece of the September Fiestas Patrias, filled with a juicy, onion-rich spiced beef pino plus a black olive, hard-boiled egg and raisins.

ingredients.name: Minced beef, or beef finely chopped by hand

steps.t: Make the pino the day before if you can, so it is cold and firm. Heat the oil in the large pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 15–20 minutes, stirring often, until very soft, sweet and translucent. Chilean pino is generous with onion; it keeps the filling juicy.

Add the beef, paprika, cumin, oregano and chilli and cook for 8 minutes, breaking up the meat, until no pink remains. Stir in the flour for 1 minute, then the stock and salt and simmer for 5 minutes. Cool, then refrigerate for at least 2 hours.

Make the dough: dissolve the salt in the warm water. Put the flour in the bowl, pour in the warm melted shortening and rub it in, then add the salted water gradually and knead for 5–8 minutes into a smooth, soft dough that doesn't stick. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 8 pieces and roll each into an oval or circle about 20 cm across and 3 mm thick. Spoon a generous 3–4 tablespoons of cold pino onto the centre and top with a piece of egg, an olive and a few raisins.

Brush the edge with water. Fold the bottom half over the filling to meet the top edge and press to seal, then fold the two sides in towards the centre and fold the top flap down over them, making the classic rectangular envelope with the seal underneath. Press well so no juices escape.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Set the empanadas on lined trays, brush with beaten egg and prick the tops once with a fork. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until deep golden brown.
Let them rest for 5–10 minutes before eating; the filling is very hot. Warn guests about the olive stone. Serve with pebre (Chilean salsa) or ensalada chilena.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate baked empanadas within 2 hours for up to 3 days, or freeze unbaked ones for up to 3 months (bake from frozen, adding 10 minutes).
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 12–15 minutes until hot through.
notes: Chilean bakers traditionally use beef fat or lard in the dough; vegetable shortening gives the same tender, flaky result.

recipes.name: Ensalada chilena (tomato and onion salad)
recipes.description: Chile's simplest and most loved salad: ripe peeled tomatoes and mild, thinly sliced onion dressed with oil, salt and coriander. The classic partner for empanadas, pastel de choclo and the asado.

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.prep: plus 1 tbsp for soaking the onion

steps.t: Slice the onion thinly lengthways (pluma style). Put it in a bowl with cold water and a tablespoon of salt, rub it between your fingers for a moment and leave it for 10–15 minutes, then rinse and drain well. This 'desflemar' step removes the harsh bite, leaving it sweet and crisp.
Peel the tomatoes: cut a shallow cross in the base of each, plunge them into boiling water for 20–30 seconds until the skin starts to curl, then into iced water. The skins slip off easily.
Cut the tomatoes into thin half-moons and arrange them on the serving dish with the onion on top.
Just before serving, season with salt, drizzle with the oil and scatter over the coriander and green chilli, if using. Toss gently at the table so the tomatoes don't break up.

recipes.storage: Best dressed just before serving; keep undressed in the fridge for a few hours.

recipes.name: Anzac biscuits
recipes.description: Golden oat and coconut biscuits sweetened with golden syrup and brown sugar, made for Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand. Bake them briefly for chewy or longer for crunchy.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 170 °C and line the baking trays with baking paper. Mix the oats, flour, coconut and brown sugar in the large bowl.
Melt the butter and golden syrup in the small saucepan over low heat, stirring, until smooth. Take off the heat.

Stir the bicarbonate of soda into the boiling water, then pour it into the butter mixture. It will foam up dramatically; this is what gives the biscuits their light, crackly texture. Pour it straight into the dry ingredients and mix well with a spoon.
Roll level tablespoons of the mixture into balls (about 25 g each) and place them on the trays 5 cm apart, then flatten them slightly with your fingers. They spread as they bake.
Bake for 12–15 minutes, until deep golden brown: 12 minutes gives chewy biscuits, 15 minutes crisp ones. They will still feel soft when they come out of the oven.
Leave the biscuits on the trays for 5 minutes to firm up, then move them to the wire rack to cool completely. Serve with a cup of tea.

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 weeks; they were made to keep.

recipes.name: Pavlova
recipes.description: A large meringue with a crisp shell and soft, marshmallowy centre, piled with whipped cream, passion fruit, kiwi fruit and strawberries. The summer and Christmas dessert of Australia and New Zealand.
equipment: Large, very clean glass or metal bowl

steps.t: Heat the oven to 120 °C. Draw a 22 cm circle on a sheet of baking paper, turn it over and lay it on the baking tray. Wipe the bowl and whisk with a little vinegar on kitchen paper: any trace of grease or yolk stops egg whites whipping.
Whisk the egg whites with the salt on medium speed until they form soft peaks that just flop over when you lift the whisk.

Turn the mixer to high and add the sugar a spoonful at a time, waiting a few seconds between additions. Keep whisking for 8–10 minutes after the last addition, until the meringue is very thick and glossy, holds stiff peaks and feels smooth, not gritty, when rubbed between your fingers. Undissolved sugar weeps syrup in the oven.
Sprinkle over the cornflour, vinegar and vanilla and whisk briefly to combine. These give the pavlova its soft, marshmallow-like centre.

Spoon the meringue onto the circle and spread it with the palette knife into a thick round with slightly raised edges and a shallow dip in the middle for the cream. Make swirls or ridges up the sides if you like.

Bake for 1 hour 15 minutes, until crisp and dry on the outside and pale cream in colour; it should lift off the paper cleanly. Turn the oven off and leave the pavlova inside with the door ajar until completely cool, about 2 hours or overnight. Cooling slowly stops it cracking and collapsing.

Just before serving, whip the cream with the icing sugar to soft peaks. Pile it onto the pavlova, top with the strawberries and kiwi fruit and spoon over the passion fruit pulp. Serve straight away, as the cream softens the meringue.

recipes.storage: Keep the plain meringue airtight at room temperature for up to 2 days. Once topped, eat within a few hours; refrigerate any leftovers and eat within 1 day.

recipes.name: Aussie meat pie
recipes.description: Australia's national pie: minced beef in a thick, peppery gravy with Worcestershire sauce, baked in a shortcrust base under a flaky puff-pastry lid. Serve with tomato sauce.

steps.t: Make the filling, ideally the day before: heat the oil in the frying pan over high heat and brown the mince in two batches for about 4 minutes each, breaking it up, until well coloured. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes until soft. Spoon off excess fat if there is a lot.

Sprinkle over the flour and stir for 1 minute, then gradually stir in the stock, tomato paste, Worcestershire sauce, soy sauce, pepper, nutmeg and salt. Simmer uncovered for 25–30 minutes, stirring often, until the gravy is thick enough to hold a trail. Cool the filling completely; hot filling melts pastry and gives a soggy base.

Make the shortcrust: rub the butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs. Sprinkle over the iced water and bring it together with a knife into a dough, adding a few drops more water if needed. Flatten into a disc, wrap and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 210 °C with the baking tray inside. Roll the shortcrust out to 3 mm thick and line the greased pie dish, pressing it into the corners; trim the edge. Chill for 15 minutes.

Spoon the cold filling into the case and level it. Brush the pastry rim with egg, lay the puff pastry sheet over the top and press the edges together firmly. Trim, crimp with a fork and cut two small steam holes in the centre. Brush the top with beaten egg.

Set the pie on the hot tray (it helps crisp the base) and bake for 35–40 minutes, until the lid is puffed and deep golden and the base is cooked: lift the edge gently with a knife and it should be golden, not pale.
Rest the pie for 10 minutes before cutting so the gravy settles. Serve hot with tomato sauce, mashed potato and peas, or, Adelaide-style, floating in a bowl of pea soup.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours for up to 3 days, or freeze the baked pie for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 180 °C oven for 20–25 minutes until the centre is steaming hot; the microwave softens the pastry.

recipes.name: Damper (Australian bush bread)
recipes.description: A simple soda bread of the Australian bush, traditionally baked in the coals of a campfire: a crusty, scored round with a soft, scone-like crumb, eaten warm with butter and golden syrup.
equipment: Baking tray or a cast-iron camp oven

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C and dust the baking tray with flour. (At a campfire, grease a cast-iron camp oven and let the fire burn down to a good bed of hot coals.)
Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt in the bowl. Rub in the butter with your fingertips until the mixture looks like breadcrumbs.
Make a well, pour in the milk and mix with the table knife, cutting through the flour, until it comes together into a soft, slightly sticky dough. Don't overmix.

Tip the dough onto a floured surface and knead it very lightly, just 4 or 5 times, until it holds together and is smooth on the underside. Overworking makes damper tough. Shape it into a round about 18 cm across and 4–5 cm thick.
Set it on the tray, cut a deep cross in the top with a floured knife and dust with a little more flour. The cross helps the heat reach the centre so it bakes evenly.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, until risen and golden and the base sounds hollow when tapped. (In a camp oven, set it in the coals with more coals on the lid for about 30 minutes.)
Cool on a rack for 10 minutes, then break or cut into wedges and serve warm with butter and golden syrup, or with soup or a barbecue.

recipes.storage: Best on the day. Wrap and keep at room temperature for 1 day; it's good toasted the next day.
recipes.reheating: Warm, wrapped in foil, in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes.

recipes.name: Kokoda (Fijian coconut-lime fish)
recipes.description: Fiji's refreshing raw fish dish: cubes of firm white fish marinated briefly in lime juice, then folded into fresh coconut cream with tomato, cucumber, onion and chilli.

ingredients.name: Very fresh, sashimi-grade firm white fish (walu, mahi-mahi or snapper)
Lime or lemon juice (from about 8 limes)
Fresh chilli (bongo chilli or bird's eye)

steps.t: Keep the fish very cold. Cut it into 1.5–2 cm cubes and put them in the glass bowl with the salt. Pour over enough lime juice to just cover the fish and stir gently.

Cover and refrigerate for 10–20 minutes, stirring once, until the outside of each cube has turned white and opaque while the centre is still slightly translucent. Fijian cooks leave it longer, up to an hour, if they like it firmer.

While the fish marinates, prepare the vegetables: scoop the seeds out of the tomatoes and cucumber so they don't water down the dressing, then dice them, the onion and the pepper into small, even pieces about 5 mm across. Keep them chilled.
Tip the fish into the sieve and drain off most of the lime juice, keeping about 2 tablespoons with the fish. The juice has done its work; too much makes the coconut cream taste sour.
Return the fish to the bowl and gently fold in the coconut cream, onion, tomato, cucumber, pepper and chilli. Taste and add a pinch more salt if needed.
Scatter with coriander and serve straight away, chilled, in bowls or coconut shells, as a starter or a light lunch with boiled cassava, taro or rice.

recipes.storage: Eat within a few hours of making it, kept chilled; don't keep leftovers.

recipes.name: Palusami (coconut cream baked in greens)
recipes.description: Samoan parcels of tender greens wrapped around rich coconut cream and onion, baked until soft, silky and custard-like. Taro leaves are traditional; large spinach leaves work well.
equipment: 6 small bowls to shape the parcels

ingredients.name: Large spinach or young taro leaves

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Mix the coconut cream, onion and salt (and lemon juice, if using) in the mixing bowl.

Cut six 30 cm squares of foil. Lay a square in a small bowl so it forms a cup, then layer 10–12 spinach leaves inside, overlapping them so there are no gaps and the leaves hang over the edge. Use the largest leaves on the outside.

Pour a sixth of the coconut mixture into the leaf cup. Fold the overhanging leaves over the top to enclose it completely, adding a leaf or two to patch any holes, then gather the foil up around the parcel and twist it tightly to seal. Repeat to make six parcels.
Set the parcels on the baking tray and bake for 45 minutes, until the leaves are very soft and the coconut cream has thickened into a rich, silky custard with a little oil separating out.

Leave for 5 minutes, then open the foil carefully, as hot steam escapes. Serve as a side with baked taro, breadfruit or sweet potato, and grilled fish or chicken, spooning the coconut sauce over everything.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: If you use real taro leaves, cook them thoroughly: raw taro leaves contain calcium oxalate crystals that irritate the mouth and throat.
A popular Samoan variation adds a spoonful of canned corned beef (pisupo) to each parcel.
